topics.title: What is Science
topics.content:
Image: scijinks.gov

Science is the study of everything around us. Science goes beyond our world, into space. With science, people have saved lives and made many other scientific advancements.

Science is a big, complicated process. But we can all understand how science is done. We will learn some really interesting things along the way.

Scientists use three things to learn about the physical and natural world. They are:

• observation (looking at things)

• research (gathering information)

• experiments (trying things to see what happens)

Scientists want to be sure their facts are correct. They use careful systems to test their ideas. This is the scientific method.

topics.title: The Scientific Method
topics.content:
The scientific method is a way to ask and answer questions about what you observe.

Creating experiments and analyzing results can be very complicated. You will not be expected to know all about it. But you should be able to explain the steps of the scientific method and create examples.

Here are the steps of the scientific method:

Steps of the Scientific Method Explained + Steps of the Scientific Method Observation Observation is the act of noticing and describing events or processes in a systematic way. This can involve using the senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell) or tools like microscopes and cameras. Observation is the first step in the scientific method, setting the stage for questions, hypotheses, and eventual experimentation. Ask a Question The scientific method starts when you ask a question about something that you observe: How, What, When, Who, Which, Why, or Where? For a science fair project some teachers require that the question be something you can measure, preferably with a number. Do Background Research Rather than starting from scratch in putting together a plan for answering your question, you want to be a savvy scientist using library and Internet research to help you find the best way to do things and ensure that you don't repeat mistakes from the past. Construct a Hypothesis A hypothesis is an educated guess about how things work. It is an attempt to answer your question with an explanation that can be tested. A good hypothesis allows you to then make a prediction: "If [I do this] , then [this] will happen." State both your hypothesis and the resulting prediction you will be testing. Predictions must be easy to measure. Test Your Hypothesis by Doing an Experiment Your experiment tests whether your prediction is accurate and thus your hypothesis is supported or not. It is important for your experiment to be a fair test. You conduct a fair test by making sure that you change only one factor at a time while keeping all other conditions the same. You should also repeat your experiments several times to make sure that the first results weren't just an accident. Analyze Your Data and Draw a Conclusion Once your experiment is complete, you collect your measurements and analyze them to see if they support your hypothesis or not. Scientists often find that their predictions were not accurate and their hypothesis was not supported, and in such cases they will communicate the results of their experiment and then go back and construct a new hypothesis and prediction based on the information they learned during their experiment. This starts much of the process of the scientific method over again. Even if they find that their hypothesis was supported, they may want to test it again in a new way. Communicate Your Results To complete your science fair project you will communicate your results to others in a final report and/or a display board. Professional scientists do almost exactly the same thing by publishing their final report in a scientific journal or by presenting their results on a poster or during a talk at a scientific meeting. In a science fair, judges are interested in your findings regardless of whether or not they support your original hypothesis.

topics.title: What is a Hypothesis
topics.content:
The diagram on the previous page includes the word “ hypothesis” (plural: hypotheses). A hypothesis is a guess based on information: what some people call “an educated guess”.

Here is an example of a hypothesis.

You observe that a cup of tea is too hot to drink. But after ten minutes it has cooled to a good drinking temperature. Your question is why?

Your hypothesis (guess) may be that tea cools over time.

You can test this hypothesis by observing two more cups of tea and finding that the tea does get cooler. You may apply your hypothesis to other hot liquids and even hot food. You observe that the liquids and solids eventually reach room temperature.

However, if you have an ice cube, it will get warmer when it is taken out of the freezer. It will melt. With this information, you might hypothesize that objects colder than room temperature will warm up until they reach room temperature. When your tests show that this hypothesis is also correct, you may form another hypothesis: liquids and solids always cool down or heat up to room temperature.

Scientists often find that their hypotheses are wrong. This is not a failure. Getting rid of wrong ideas helps scientists get closer to the truth. Even when scientists say a hypothesis is “correct” or “confirmed,” they are willing to be proved wrong.  That’s because some future scientists might discover a new idea that shows an accepted fact in a new light.

GED EXAM TIP: HOW TO APPLY THE SCIENTIFIC METHOD In your science test, you will need to answer questions that test your knowledge of the scientific method. Before you take your science test, you should understand and remember the 7 steps and what they represent. Then you will be able to recognize examples when they come up in your test. Also, you will be able to apply the steps if you are asked to create and analyze an experiment. So your test tip for this lesson is to memorize the steps of the scientific method. Look back and review the steps for the scientific method, then you can easily recognize or apply them in your test. The scientific method is a systematic approach to inquiry that scientists use to explore observations, answer questions, and test hypotheses. Here are the seven steps of the scientific method: ■ Check for understanding Let’s read a story about drinking water. Then we’ll apply the scientific method to it. Water quality in Joseph’s community Joseph lives in Glendale, where people are getting a stomach bug called Giardiasis. Many of Joseph’s neighbors have been getting sick, but not all of them. He wonders why some of them are not infected. Joseph asks around and finds out that his healthy neighbors always boil their drinking water. Joseph reads about Giardiasis and finds out it comes from Giardia. Giardia is the name of a bug that sometimes gets into water systems. He also reads that many bugs cannot live in boiling water. He wonders if the boiling water kills the Giardia bug. Joseph decides to check and see. He collects water from his faucet and divides it into two jars. He boils the water in one container. Then Joseph buys a water test kit and tests the water in both jars. The unboiled water was infected with Giardia bugs. The boiled water had no live bugs. Joseph quickly puts a notice on the community Facebook page: Boil your water before you drink it! Seven steps of the Scientific Method: Question : Ask a question about a problem or phenomenon Research : Do background research to learn what is already known about the topic Hypothesis : Create an educated guess, or potential explanation, based on prior research Experiment : Conduct a controlled experiment to test the hypothesis Data Analysis : Analyze the data from the experiment Conclusion : Draw a conclusion about the hypothesis based on the findings Communication : Share the results Can you match the steps in the diagram to Joseph’s story? Answer : Observation : Lots of Joseph’s neighbors have been getting sick, but not all of them. Question : He wonders why some of them are not infected. Background research: 1) Joseph asks around and finds out that his healthy neighbors always boil their drinking water. 2) Joseph reads about Giardiasis and finds out it comes from the bug Giardia. 3) He also reads that many bugs cannot live in boiling water. Form hypothesis : He wonders if the boiling water kills the Giardia bug. Test with experiment : He collects water from his faucet and divides it into two jars. He boils the water in one container. Analyze results : Joseph buys a water test kit and tests the water in both jars. The

unboiled water was infected with Giardia bugs. The boiled water had no live bugs. Report results: Joseph quickly puts a notice on the community Facebook page – Boil your water before you drink it!

topics.title: What is Data
topics.content:
Data refers to any collection of facts, numbers, words, measurements, observations, or even just descriptions of things. It is raw, unprocessed information that can be used for analysis, research,

decision-making, and more. Scientists use data to make conclusions and share results.

Numbers are one kind of data . But data is more than just numbers.

Some examples of data:

• The records of the high and low temperatures each day

• The names of all the people who have been president of Nicaragua, or any other country

• You have data connected to you. You have a name, a date of birth, and a height. All of these are examples of data.

• Number of people in your house, neighborhood, or community, is also a form of data

Collecting or finding data often starts with a question. It could be anything from “How often does the sunshine in my city?” to “How does my government spend its money?” to “What is the fastest route to the grocery store?”

topics.title: Types of Data
topics.content:
The two major types of data are qualitative and quantitative:

Qualitative data is information about descriptive characteristics or “quality”. Descriptions of color, texture or a process are all qualitative data. You can put qualitative data into a category. You can categorize data in many ways.

For example, a soccer ball can be categorized as mini, small, or used. People might be babies, children, or adults. Test questions might be in the difficult category or the easy category.

Quantitative data is information about a quantity or number.

Examples: The number of soccer balls, the birth weight of infants, the price of flour, and a score on a test are all quantitative data.

topics.title: Variables
topics.content:
Variables are things that can vary, or change. Some variables reflect a change over time. The temperature at noon is a variable because it varies from day to day, depending on the weather and time of year. If you collect this data for many years, you can predict the temperature at noon for a particular date. You would base your prediction on how warm and cold it has been on that same date in the past.

When a measurement changes from subject to subject, it is also a variable. Height is a variable because it changes from person to person. There are two types of variables:

• Independent variables are the ones you start within an experiment. These are independent of what happens in the experiment. Scientists may apply or change variables to see what effect they have.

• Dependent variables are what you want to learn about by performing your experiment. They are changes that depend on the independent variables.

Here are some examples of the two types of variables:

Example 1: Plant Growth Independent Variable : Amount of water given to the plants. Dependent Variable : Growth of the plants (measured by height, number of leaves, etc.).

Example 2: Study Time and Test Scores Independent Variable: Amount of time spent studying. Dependent Variable : Scores on the test.

Example 3: Exercise and Weight Loss Independent Variable: Duration of exercise sessions. Dependent Variable: Amount of weight lost.

topics.title: Control Groups
topics.content:
When scientists test medicines, they often use control groups to make sure that they are seeing real results.

A control group, also known as a controlled or constant variable, is used for comparison. Joseph’s water quality experiment used unboiled water so he could compare the boiled water. In another example, a control group could be a group of people who do not get the medicine being tested.

A group people can also be a control group in a research

Example 1: Medication Effectiveness Study Objective : To test the effectiveness of a new drug in lowering blood pressure.

Experimental Group : This group receives the new drug. Control Group : This group receives a placebo (a pill with no active ingredient). In this example, the control group helps to determine whether changes in blood pressure are due to the new drug or some other factor, such as the placebo effect.

Example 2: Fertilizer on Plant Growth Study Objective : To determine if a new type of fertilizer increases plant growth.

Experimental Group: This group of plants receives the new fertilizer. Control Group: This group of plants receives no fertilizer or the standard fertilizer. By comparing the growth of plants in the experimental group to those in the control group, researchers can assess the effectiveness of the new fertilizer.

topics.title: Using Samples
topics.content:
When you collect data, you can’t always measure everything. For example, to find the average human height in 2018, you would not measure every single person in the world! Instead, you would measure the height of a sample of people.

A sample is a small quantity of the thing you are measuring. Again, remember the water quality experiment in the last lesson. The water Joseph collected was a sample.

Sampling is an important part of conducting research. You have to decide how many tests to perform, or people to observe, or places from which to collect data.

Random samples

Illustration of a simple random sample (Courtesy: www.geeksforgeeks.org)

Random samples help scientists collect accurate data. A random sample means that each object in the sample has an equal chance of being chosen from the overall set of objects being studied. For example, a farmer wants to know how many insects are in his apple orchards. He would not have a good sample if he only selected trees near the road. A better option is to randomly select the trees from all over the orchard.

topics.title: Showing Data
topics.content:
You can show data in words, numbers, or using pictures called diagrams . People often understand data better when they can see it. Diagrams showing number data are called graphs or charts. They make it easy to see patterns in data and find information.

Line Graphs

A line graph is good at showing continuous data. Scientists often use line graphs to show the results of their experiments. With a line graph, they can show the relationship between variables.

LearnDash Line Graph

Above is an example of a line graph showing the number of luxury cars sold by a dealer between January and July

Charts Charts are a kind of graph. You can use charts to show information in categories. Hair color, types of fruits, or countries where people were born are variables that are also categories. Charts are not good for continuous data, like line graphs. They present data that can be counted in separate chunks.

LearnDash Bar Chart

One example of a chart is a histogram, which is a type of bar chart.

Bar charts show data in bars of different heights. On a regular bar chart, each bar shows one variable, such as the types of fruit sold. On a histogram, the bars show groups, or ranges – for example, the number of shirts of different colors sold over a period.

GED Exam Tip: How to read a Line Graph You will see several graphs and charts in your GED Science exam. To answer questions about them, you need to know what they are about and how to read the data in them. A good graph always has a clear title that tells you what it is about. It will have labels for different parts, too. It may also have a key to explain colors or shapes used in the graph. In your science test, carefully read the title, labels, and key to understand what the graph is showing you. The title of the graph below says it is about the height of people around the world over a period of time. The labels tell us that one set of numbers shows the year, and the other set of numbers shows the height of people in centimeters. The horizontal (across the page) line of a graph is called the x-axis. The vertical (up the page) line of the graph is called the y–axis. The axes of the graph show the variables. Usually, the independent variable will be on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y–axis. This makes it easy to see how the dependent variable changes as the independent variable changes. On our graph, the independent variable, on the x-axis, is years. The dependent variable, on the y–axis, is people’s height. There are a lot of colored lines on the graph. The key under the graph explains what each color means. In this graph, each color stands for a different region of the world. Now that we understand what the graph is showing, let’s learn how to analyze the information in it. The lines on the graph show certain patterns. One pattern is that all of the lines have risen from the beginning. This shows that the average height of all people increased between 1810 and 1980. You can get details from the graph, too. The purple line representing Eastern Europe and Central Asia shows that the average height in that region in 1810 was less than 165 cm. In 1980, the average height in the same region was more than 175 cm.

Doctors want to find out if protein supplements help their patients recovering from knee surgery. A group of 20 patients recovering from knee surgery is divided into 2 groups of 10 patients each. The 10 patients in Group 1 were given protein supplements. The patients in Group 2 were given no protein supplements.
This table shows how many days each patient in each group took to recover. When the doctors analyzed the data in this table, they found that their patients recovered more quickly on average when they were given protein supplements.
QUESTION
:
Is the doctors’ conclusion true or false?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
a) True
Explanation:
Step 1:
First let’s make sure we understand what the table is telling us. The column on the left lists ten numbers. Are these numbers of patients? The number of supplements? Let’s stop and read the column heading carefully. It says Group 1 (received supplements) number of recovery days. So the numbers in the column are the numbers of days patients took to recover. The same goes for the right–hand column – these are the numbers of recovery days for patients who did not get the supplements.
Step 2:
Now that we understand the data, let’s look at the question. Is it true or false that the patients recovered more quickly on average with supplements? What does “on average” mean? It means we need to figure out the average recovery time of each group to get the answer. We need to calculate the mean.
Step 3:
Now that we understand what we are being asked, let’s do the math! There are 10 patients in each group, so let’s add up Group 1’s recovery days and divide it by 10: 61 total recovery hours divided by 10: 61/10 = 6.1 days average.
Now let’s do Group 2: 70 total recovery hours divided by 10; 70/10 = 7 days average.
Group 1(with supplements) : 6.1 days average
Group 2 (without supplements): 7 days average
It seems based on average recovery time that the answer is true: the supplements did help the patients to recover more quickly, by almost a whole day on average.

topics.title: 3 Kinds of Averages
topics.content:
One skill you will need for your test is being able to calculate an average .

An average is a value that summarizes or represents a group of numbers. It can be calculated in different ways, depending on what you want to know about the set. Here are the most common types of averages:

• Mean : The most commonly used average, which gives you a general idea of the overall group. You find the mean by adding all the numbers in the set together and dividing by the number of items.

• Median : The middle value in a set when the numbers are arranged in order. If the set has an even number of items, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

• Mode : The most frequent number in the set—the number that appears most often.

Another important concept is range , which measures the spread of the numbers. It is the difference between the largest and smallest values in a set. For example, in the set (6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 11, 12), the range is calculated by subtracting the smallest number (6) from the largest number (12), resulting in a range of 6.

How might this show up in a test?

You will likely need to calculate the mean , but questions could also involve finding the median or mode , or determining the range . These problems might be presented as word problems, through tables of numbers, or as a combination of both.

It's important to know how to calculate each of these to be well-prepared for your test.

It may seem obvious now that we, and other living things, are made up of cells. Prior to the 1600s, however, it wasn’t obvious at all, for the simple reason that no one had ever seen a cell up close and personal. To distinguish individual cells in a piece of tissue or individual bacteria in a sample of liquid required the development of relatively high–powered microscopes, instruments used for magnifying objects otherwise too small to be seen. For more on how microscopes are used in biology today, check out the article on microscopy.
The first person to observe cells as microscopic structures was the British scientist Robert Hooke. In fact, he was the person who gave cells their name. In his book Micrographia, he used the term cell to refer to the box–like structures he saw when he looked at dead cork tissue through a simple microscope. He chose the cell as the name because these boxes reminded him of the cells of a monastery, the simple rooms in which monks slept.
The cells that Hooke observed, however, were in dead tissue, and were in fact cell walls left behind after the death of the real cells. The first person to observe living, moving cells was Anton van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch shopkeeper and crafter of lenses. In the 1670s, inspired by Hooke’s book, he began to build his own, more powerful microscopes. With these, he was able to observe living single–celled organisms—such as bacteria—and sperm cells, which he collectively called animalcules.

topics.title: What is Biology?
topics.content:
Biology is the study of living organisms and their interactions with each other and their environments. It covers a wide range of topics, including the structure, function, growth, evolution, and distribution of all forms of life, from microscopic bacteria to large animals and plants.

Biologists explore how organisms develop, reproduce, and respond to their surroundings, helping us understand the complexity and diversity of life on Earth.

topics.title: What is a cell?
topics.content:
Source: technologynetworks.com

A cell is the basic building block of all living things. Think of it like a tiny room that makes up a bigger structure.

Cells are so small that you can’t see them without a microscope. They have different parts inside that do specific jobs to keep the cell, and the organism it's part of, alive.

Some living things, like bacteria, are made of just one cell. Others, like humans, are made of trillions of cells working together.

Types of cells

There are two types of cells: prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells.

• Prokaryotic cells

Bacteria are the smallest and most numerous organisms on the planet. Bacteria are unicellular and have no nucleus. This simple cell is called a prokaryotic cell. They multiply constantly by dividing the cell in a process called binary fission (which means splitting in two).

• Eukaryotic cells

Eukaryotic cells make plants, animals, and a few other types of living things. Eukaryotic cells have many different jobs to do. A brain cell in your body, for example, has an entirely different job than the cell in a leaf that makes food for the plant.

topics.title: Structure of Eukaryotic Cells
topics.content:
Now let’s look at the structure of cells. All eukaryotic cells are made of the same basic parts. Here are some of them:

• The nucleus is the cell’s headquarters. It controls what the cell does and how it is made.

• Chromosomes hold the information that tells the cell what it is and how to behave.

• Cytoplasm surrounds the nucleus. It holds various smaller parts.

• Mitochondria (plural of mitochondria) process oxygen and food to make energy, in the form of ATP, for the cell.

• The cell membrane is like skin. It controls what goes in or out of the cell.

There are other parts to cells as well as those labeled above. Any parts that have a function are called organelles. For example, a mitochondrion and a nucleus are organelles. Another organelle is a ribosome, which makes protein for the cell to use.

Plant cells have additional organelles such as chloroplasts and cell walls . Chloroplasts convert light energy into food for the plant in a process called photosynthesis. Cell walls are made out of repeating units of glucose molecules (called cellulose) that provide an additional layer of protection for the cell.

This picture shows some of the types of cells in humans. All these calls have the same basic structure inside, even though they look different and act in different ways.

Same structure, different jobs

Although all cells start with the same parts, they take many shapes and perform many different jobs. The cell we looked at above is a basic animal cell. It could become a muscle cell, a liver cell, a blood cell, or a nerve cell. It could be inside a human or a snail. There are more than 250 types of cells in the human body. Other living things have cells with different functions.

But by the time you take your test, you should be familiar with scientific words like these. You will have to answer comprehension (understanding) questions about texts that use scientific words. The questions will test your thinking skills, not your knowledge! But if you don’t understand the text and don’t know the answer, use the steps we used here: Read the question. Then, go back to the text to find the words the question is about. Then test the answers against the text. You will find the best answer that way. ■ Check for understanding Let’s practice with a scientific text about mitochondria. Read the text below from nature.com. Choose the best answer to the question. Mitochondria are thought to have originated from an ancient symbiosis that resulted when a nucleated cell engulfed an aerobic prokaryote. The engulfed cell came to rely on the protective environment of the host cell, and, conversely, the host cell came to rely on the engulfed prokaryotic for energy production. Over time, the descendants of the engulfed prokaryotic developed into mitochondria, and the work of these

organelles — using oxygen to create energy — became critical to eukaryotic evolution. In the passage above, what organism relied on the protective environment of the host cell? A. the ancient symbiosis B. the descendants C. the nucleated cell. D. the aerobic prokaryote Explanation and Answer: When you read the passage, you saw many words you do not know the meaning of. But the question is using words that are in the text, so after reading the question carefully, let’s go back and find those words in the text. Here they are: The engulfed cell came to rely on the protective environment of the host cell. So we know it was the engulfed cell that relied on the protection. But “the engulfed cell” is not one of our choices! So we need to figure out which organism is the engulfed cell. Let’s look at our possible answers and test them against the text: A. Ancient symbiosis is not an organism, but even if you don’t know that, you can tell it’s not the right answer because the text doesn’t say it was engulfed. B. Descendants means the ones that came after, but even if you don’t know that, you can tell it’s not the right answer because the text doesn’t say they were engulfed. C. The nucleated cell – what does the text say about that? It says: A nucleated cell engulfed an aerobic prokaryote. You may not know what a nucleated cell is, and you may not know what engulf means, but you can tell the nucleated cell was not engulfed. It engulfed something else! D. The aerobic prokaryote – This is our last choice, so let’s check that D is the right answer. The text says “A nucleated cell engulfed an aerobic prokaryote”. This tells us the aerobic prokaryote is the engulfed cell. It is the organism we are looking for. D is the best answer. (By the way, engulf means surround and swallow up) Of course, you may have known the correct answer right away, without testing each statement.

topics.title: How Cells Reproduce
topics.content:
In living things, cells are always changing. Every second, cells are dying and new ones are forming. We will look at two methods of cell division: mitosis and meiosis. Be sure to look over the image of similarities and differences below.

1. Mitosis

Mitosis is the process of cells splitting apart themselves, a one cell decision process. First, the nucleus splits in two. Then, the cell stretches in the middle until it splits, too. Each nucleus becomes the center of a new cell. These cells ,daughter cells, are identical. This process is called mitosis. It reproduces the whole cell, twice, with all the DNA it needs. The DNA is stored in the nucleus, where it is organized into structures called chromosomes. Your skin cells, blood cells, and muscle cells reproduce using mitosis.

2. Meiosis

Meiosis is a kind of cell division that happens in organisms that reproduce with a partner. It makes sex cells, like sperm and egg. One cell divides twice and creates four new cells. Each new cell has only half the number of chromosomes as the original cell. These sex cells are all a little different. When a sperm and egg join, they make a zygote with a full set of chromosomes—half from each parent.

Although mitosis and meiosis follow the same basic steps, they have more differences than similarities. Most of these differences relate back to the fact that, although both are needed for cell replication, mitosis and meiosis have different purposes: mitosis replaces body cells with identical copies, while meiosis creates genetically different sex cells that will be used to create an entirely new organism.

Most cells in large multicellular organisms don’t directly exchange substances like nutrients and wastes with the external environment. Microscopes and lenses
Although cells vary in size, they’re generally quite small. For instance, the diameter of a typical human red blood cell is about eight micrometers (0.008 millimeters). To give you some context, the head of a pin is about one millimeter in diameter, so about 125 red blood cells could be lined up in a row across the head of a pin. With a few exceptions, individual cells cannot be seen with the naked eye, so scientists must instead use microscopes (micro– = “small”; –scope = “to look at”) to study them. A microscope is an instrument that magnifies objects otherwise too small to be seen, producing an image in which the object appears larger. Most photographs of cells are taken using a microscope, and these pictures can also be called micrographs.
From the definition above, it might sound like a microscope is just a kind of magnifying glass. In fact, magnifying glasses do qualify as microscopes; since they have just one lens, they are called simple microscopes. The fancier instruments that we typically think of as microscopes are compound microscopes, meaning that they have multiple lenses. Because of the way these lenses are arranged, they can bend light to produce a much more magnified image than that of a magnifying glass.

“Discovering cells
:
It may seem obvious now that we, and other living things, are made up of cells. Prior to the 1600s, however, it wasn’t obvious at all, for the simple reason that no one had ever seen a cell up close and personal. To distinguish individual cells in a piece of tissue or individual bacteria in a sample of liquid required the development of relatively high–powered microscopes, instruments used for magnifying objects otherwise too small to be seen. For more on how microscopes are used in biology today, check out the article on microscopy.
The first person to observe cells as microscopic structures was the British scientist Robert Hooke. In fact, he was the person who gave cells their name. In his book Micrographia, he used the term cell to refer to the box–like structures he saw when he looked at dead cork tissue through a simple microscope. He chose the cell as the name because these boxes reminded him of the cells of a monastery, the simple rooms in which monks slept.
The cells that Hooke observed, however, were in dead tissue, and were in fact cell walls left behind after the death of the real cells. The first person to observe living, moving cells was Anton van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch shopkeeper and crafter of lenses. In the 1670s, inspired by Hooke’s book, he began to build his own, more powerful microscopes. With these, he was able to observe living single–celled organisms—such as bacteria—and sperm cells, which he collectively called animalcules.”

topics.title: Human Biology
topics.content:
Human biology is the study of how human cells, organs, and systems work. By themselves, cells are small, but together, they can create many types of tissue. Tissue makes up organs. Organs make up systems. And systems make up all living things, including humans!

topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

What are tissues and organs? Tissue is made of similar cells that group together to do a job in the body. Humans have four types of tissue: Connective tissue makes bones, blood, tendons, ligaments, and parts of organs. Muscle tissue allows you to move. Nervous tissue makes up the nervous system, which includes your brain. Epithelial tissue covers organs. Your skin is epithelial tissue, and so are your intestines. Tissues work together to make organs. Organs are self–contained units that serve a specific function in an organism. The brain, heart, liver, and lungs are all organs. The statements will agree or disagree with what is in the text, but they will use different words. The questions will test your understanding of scientific materials. Humans have four types of tissue: Connective tissue makes bones, blood, tendons, ligaments, and parts of organs. Muscle tissue allows you to move. topics.title: Skeletal & Muscular System
topics.content:
Two or more organs working together to do a specific function are called a system. The human body is made up of many systems. Here is some information about important systems in the human body.

Skeletal system

Image courtesy of interactive–biology. com

Humans have 206 bones that make their skeleton. Bones are alive, just like all the other parts of your body! There is also a network of tendons, ligaments, and cartilage connecting the skeleton. All these parts together form the skeletal system. The skeletal system supports the body, and it is essential for movement.

Muscular system

Muscles allow us to move. They attach to our bones. The muscular system provides strength, balance, posture, movement, and heat. The muscles that power the heart work automatically. Otherwise, we would think about each breath we take! An Orthopedist is a doctor who specializes in the musculoskeletal system.

topics.title: Respiratory & Cardiovascular System
topics.content:
Respiratory system

The respiratory system is all the organs and tissues that get oxygen to your tissues. Your cells need oxygen to live. When you inhale (breathe air in) your lungs take in oxygen for your body. When you exhale (breathe air out) your lungs get rid of carbon dioxide.

A Pulmonologist is a physician who specializes in the respiratory system.

These are the lungs of a non–smoker and a smoker. Cigarette smoke hurts the lungs. So does living in places with a lot of air pollution.

Cardiovascular system

The cardiovascular system carries oxygen and nutrients around the body. It also removes waste. It uses blood in a system of blood vessels (veins and arteries) to do this. The major organ of the circulatory system is the heart. The heart drives this system. First, it pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen and leaves carbon dioxide behind. Then the heart pumps blood through the body. The blood gives oxygen to cells and picks up carbon dioxide. The blood finally returns to the heart to begin its cycle again. Blood travels through the blood vessels from large arteries, to smaller arteries, to capillaries, to small veins, to large veins, and back to the heart.

A cardiologist is a doctor who specializes in treating diseases of the cardiovascular system — mainly the heart and blood vessels.

topics.title: Digestive, Urinary & Endocrine System
topics.content:
The digestive system consists of the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestines, and large intestines. The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients , which the body uses for energy.

Diagram of the human digestive system

Here are the parts of the digestive system:

• The gastrointestinal (GI) tract includes the large intestine, the small intestine, and the esophagus. It carries food through the body. It sends nutrients to the bloodstream and gets rid of waste.

• The liver does three main things: it aids in digestion, makes proteins, and gets rid of bad things.

• The pancreas helps break down food into nutrients.

• The gallbladder helps digest fat.

• A Gastroenterologist is a doctor specializing in digestive problems that affect your digestive system, which includes your esophagus, stomach, intestines, pancreas, gallbladder, and liver.

Urinary system

The urinary system gets rid of unwanted materials from your body. These include materials left after other systems have taken out the nutrients. The organs in the urinary system include the liver, the kidneys, the large intestine, the bladder, and the skin.

A urologist is a doctor who specializes in disorders of the urinary system.

Endocrine system

The endocrine system mostly deals with processes that happen slowly, such as developing bones. The endocrine system uses hormones to send messages all over the body. Hormones help to control:

• mood

• growth and development

• tissue function

• metabolism

• sexual function

• reproduction

Endocrinologists are medical doctors who specialize in diagnosing and treating health conditions related to problems with the body's hormones, hormonal glands, and related tissues.

topics.title: Nervous system
topics.content:
The brain is the control center of the nervous system. This is where thoughts, feelings, and memories reside. The nervous system is made up of billions of nerve cells, or neurons , which join together to make nerves. Nerves constantly send signals back and forth between the brain and the rest of the body.

The signals are messages that control your body’s actions. Some actions are voluntary (things you decide to do) and some are involuntary (things your body does automatically).

A Neurologist is a doctor who treats diseases of the brain and spinal cord, peripheral nerves, and muscles.

topics.title: Immune System
topics.content:
The immune system protects the body. There are many bacteria, viruses, and other organisms that can harm us. The immune system is a network of cells, tissues, and organs that work together to attack any invaders! It is what keeps us healthy. People with weak immune systems can get very sick from things that would not affect someone with a strong immune system.

The human immune system is made up of organs, cells, and proteins that work together to protect the body from invaders.

An Immunologist is a doctor who specializes in disorders of the immune system.

topics.title: DNA and RNA
topics.content:
What is DNA?

DNA , or deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for living organisms. It is often described as a blueprint or recipe for building and maintaining life.

How do cells decide whether to be a brain cell, muscle cell, or skin cell?

DNA (short for Deoxyribonucleic acid) tells the cell what to be and do.

DNA has a double-helix structure,

Inside the cell’s nucleus are strands of DNA. The DNA holds instructions, like recipes, for the cell. The strands look like two spiral ladders twisted together. This is called a double helix .

DNA makes new cells

The DNA tells the cell what to be and do, but it also tells it how to make more cells just like itself. To do this, a DNA strand gives its information to a messenger strand called RNA .

The RNA strand carries the “recipe” out of the nucleus to the ribosomes. Using the recipe, the ribosomes build proteins in just the right shape for their particular kind of cell.

This diagram shows what happens inside a cell to make it grow and do its job. It shows how information is taken from DNA inside the nucleus and turned into proteins. The red line is the messenger RNA (mRNA). The green pentagon is the ribosome. The dark blue circles are the building blocks of proteins (amino acid monomers) linked together from the information in the DNA. The proteins make the parts of cells, and cells are the tiny parts that all living things are made of!

topics.title: What are Genes?
topics.content:
We just learned that each DNA recipe makes one kind of protein. The unique recipe, or sequence of DNA, is called a gene .

Genes can make all kinds of proteins. Some proteins make hormones that affect how we feel. Other proteins create cell structures or make things happen in our bodies.

Genes give us traits

Genes also give people their traits. Traits are characteristics: things as hair color and height. But traits include tendencies, too. A tendency is something like whether you are mostly cheerful or easily depressed. Or it could be that you are more likely to put on weight than your friend who has different genes.

topics.title: Chromosomes
topics.content:
Genes (strands of DNA in a particular pattern) are stored in chromosomes . Chromosomes contain hundreds or even thousands of genes.

Chromosomes form genomes

A genome is a complete set of DNA for any organism or living thing. The human genome has 23 pairs of chromosomes. That makes 46 chromosomes. One set of 23 chromosomes comes from your mother, and one set comes from your father.

DNA makes sequences called genes. Genes are stored in packets called chromosomes. Every genome is made of a set number of chromosomes. This is the human genome: 23 pairs of chromosomes.

One special pair of chromosomes decides what sex you are. Females always have two X chromosomes, so they always give an X to their child. Males always have one X and one Y. This means the father can give either an X or a Y to a child. That X or Y decides the sex of the child.

topics.title: How Heredity Works
topics.content:
We learned that genes give us our traits, such as hair color. We also learned that we get our genes from our parents. So our traits come from our parents. This is why children look like their parents. We call this heredity.

But what if a father has black straight hair while the mother has brown curly hair?

If their children all have brown curly hair, the mother’s hair gene is most likely dominant . It was the stronger one. The father’s black hair gene was most likely the recessive gene – it stayed in the background. For a person to inherit black hair in this case, they would have to inherit two recessive alleles or genes for that trait.

topics.title: Heredity Experiment
topics.content:
In 1865, a scientist named Gregor Mendel used an experiment to show how heredity and dominant genes work.

Mendel used peas for his experiment. Just like people, peas get one copy of DNA from each parent pea! Peas can be green (G) or yellow (Y). A pea with two yellow genes (YY) is yellow, and a pea with two green genes (GG) is green. But what happens if a pea is YG? One of the genes is dominant. The dominant gene controls whether it is green or yellow.

Let’s look at this in a diagram.

This diagram shows the genetics of peas. Allele means the gene version the pea has. Look at how the YG in the second row can produce YYs, YGs, or GGs.

In the diagram above, Y is dominant, so peas with both a Y and G are yellow. If a YY pea breeds with a GG pea, the first generation of their offspring is all YG because they get one copy from each. But in later generations, there are other possibilities. This is because sometimes the G is passed on from a YG pea. That means a pea that looks yellow is passing on its green allele. If that green pairs with another green, then it is a GG and will produce a green pea.

Before the discovery of genetics, people were confused as to how a green pea could come from yellow pea parents!

topics.title: Video: Punnett Squares
topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

The Punnett square is a square diagram that is used to predict the genotypes of a particular cross or breeding experiment. It is named after Reginald C. Punnett, who devised the approach in 1905. The diagram is used by biologists to determine the probability of an offspring having a particular genotype. The processes of meiosis and fertilization can be summarized in Punnett squares to make predictions about the genotypes and phenotypes of offspring. These predictions are accurate for large samples, but random variation in the genetic makeup of the sperm and egg that unite to form each zygote often results in substantial discrepancies between the Punnett square predictions and the outcomes observed in small samples such as individual families. Each fertilization event is independent of other fertilization events, so the genetic makeup of each child is independent of the genetic makeup of any siblings. Punnett squares are a useful model for understanding how meiosis and fertilization result in the various possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring. Pedigrees are a useful model for analyzing inheritance in individual families. While Punnett squares are a convenient tool to understand Mendelian genetics, they cannot be used in many situations involving complex genetic inheritance. For example, they are not effective in estimating the distribution of genotypes and phenotypes when there is a linkage between two genes. Sometimes, let’s use flowers, for example, the genes splice or “blend” we get multicolor variations where we normally wouldn’t. Often breeders will mate animals in multiple cycles to achieve the rare or unusual combinations as well. For the test, all punnett squares will work as theoretically expected. You will probably get a question based on Mendel’s experiment in your test. Questions about heredity often ask you to predict what will happen. Let’s practice a hereditary question. Brown eyes (shown as B) are dominant over blue eyes (shown as b). If someone has a brown–eye gene and a blue–eye gene (Bb), they will have brown eyes. They will only have blue eyes if both genes are blue (bb). A Punnett square is a diagram that shows the possible traits that offspring could have based on the genes they get from their parents. This Punnett square shows the possible eye colors for a child born from parents who are both Bb. One parent’s set of eye color genes are on the left. The other parent’s eye color genes are along the top. They can both give either one of their eye color genes to their child. The possible combinations they make are shown in the four squares with two letters. ■ Check for understanding Using the Punnett square listed above, how likely is it that a child of these two parents will have brown eyes? Explanations and Answer: You can answer questions about heredity if you remember the basic rules you learned about genes: (1) children get one set of genes from each parent (2) if one of the pair of genes for a trait is dominant, that will be the one that shows in the child. Now that you’ve reminded yourself of the rules, look at the diagram again to see how many squares make a brown-eyed child. Brown (B) is dominant, so anywhere there is a B, the eyes will

be brown. Three out of the four squares have a B, so the answer is three out of four. Only the combination with the blue bb will make a blue-eyed child. In BB and Bb, the brown gene is dominant and will give the child brown eyes. Three out of four (¾) is the same as 75%. There is a 75% likelihood a child of two parents will have brown eyes. Apply the basic rules to any heredity question in your test, and they should help you choose the right answer.

topics.title: Categories of Organisms
topics.content:
Scientists separate all organisms into groups. These groups, called categories, help define species. A species is a group of living things that are alike and breed (reproduce) with each other.

This chart shows the biggest categories of life on Earth: kingdom, phylum, and class. In the top row, you can see that Animalia is one of the kingdoms. The middle row shows all the phyla that are in the Animalia kingdom. One of the phyla is Chordata, which includes all the classes you can see in the bottom row.

Let’s take a look at the seven categories, starting at the top with the biggest groups:

• Kingdoms are the broadest category. The kingdom category includes plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria. Within those kingdoms are smaller categories. Animalia contains humans and all other animals.

• Phylum is the physical type of an animal. Birds and mammals are in the phylum Chordata.

• Class divides Chordata into mammals, fish, reptiles, birds, and more. Humans are mammals (Mammalia in the chart above).

• Order is the next level. Orders of mammals include carnivores, a mammal that eats meat. Humans are in the order called primates, which have large brains.

• Family narrows even more. Humans and large apes are in the family Hominidae.

• Genus is the level that families are split into. Humans are in the genus Homo, which once included other kinds of humans that died out long ago.

• A Species is a group of living things that are alike and can reproduce with each other. Humans are homo sapiens, the only species of humans alive today.

topics.title: How does evolution occur?
topics.content:
The word evolution means development or change over time.

Evolution happens when traits are passed down from one generation to the next. Sometimes, over many generations, the traits change a little due to cellular mutation. The theory of evolution says this is how species develop.

So how can they change?

Over time, DNA changes as it gets passed down. Certain traits mutate and become more biologically fit. One species can even become two species. It takes many years for a whole species to change or turn into new species.

Illustration of how humans may have evolved

topics.title: Natural Selection
topics.content:
Evolution happens because some members of a species survive better than others. This could be a plant or bird with traits that help it to survive better than another plant or bird. They are more fit – which in evolution means they have more offspring (babies). If they have more offspring, their traits will be passed on more often. So the species will evolve through natural selection.

Here is an example of natural selection .

In many bird species, females choose males with the most colorful feathers. The males may not be stronger or faster, but their bright colors attract females. So the most colorful males produce more offspring than less colorful males. The colorful males have higher fitness.

As more colorful birds reproduce and share their DNA and their traits, the next generation has more color. The species is slowly changing to favor colorful birds.

Here is another example.

A fast snow leopard can kill more prey. She will eat more than a slow leopard, so she is healthier and will have more babies. Her fast genes will pass to more leopards.

In both examples, the traits that make them more fit will be passed down to more offspring through genes.

Artificial selection

Farmers have learned how to use selection to make better food. They choose the fittest members of species to reproduce.

This is called artificial selection . For example, wheat evolved from much smaller wild grasses. Farmers choose the plants with the largest seeds to replant every year. Over thousands of years, wheat now has much larger seeds than wild grass would.

Mutations and adaptations

Evolution can also happen by accident. Sometimes DNA can get copied incorrectly. This is called a mutation . Mutations are very small. Sometimes many mutations are required to produce a visible change.

An adaptation is a mutation that helps organisms be better suited to their environment. If a mutation makes an organism more fit, then natural selection will take place, and the mutation will stay in the species.

topics.title: How New Species Appear
topics.content:
One species can become two species through selection, mutations, or adaptations. The two new species are not able to breed with each other. This is called speciation .

This picture shows speciation. The country of Panama lies between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Millions of years ago, Panama was covered by water, and shrimp lived there.

Over millions of years, a strip of land formed that is today called Panama. It created a barrier between the bodies of water. Today, the two sides of Panama have different species of shrimp. Because their environments were no longer the same, the shrimp adapted in different ways. After a while (more millions of years!) speciation split the shrimp into new species.

topics.title: Today’s Species
topics.content:
Evolution tells us that all organisms came from one ancestor. Adaptation, natural selection, and speciation have created the many types of plants, animals, and other organisms we see today.

In this phylogeny chart, each dot represents an ancestor shared between the groups. For example, this chart shows that long ago, elephants were related to lungfish! Image courtesy of Understanding Evolution.

Scientists can compare DNA to find out if different organisms are related to each other. This is called phylogeny – the study of how living things evolved.

The mammals with white fur had a disadvantage in producing offspring. B. The mammals with brown fur had an advantage in producing offspring. C. Explanation and Answer: To answer this question, you can use some of the tips you have learned so far. You’ve learned to read line graphs. It shows the fur colors of mammals. The key tells you which line shows which color. It has no numbers! It's just showing you if the percentage in the population of each color went up, went down, or stayed the same over time. That’s all you need to know. Now look at the question. Notice it doesn’t ask which statement is right. It asks which statement is the most likely explanation for what the data shows. It is asking you to draw a conclusion from the data. Now test the statements. You will find that C is the most likely explanation because the line showing the percentage of the population with white fur went up, while the other lines went down or stayed about the same. It helps support the claim that white fur has a reproductive advantage. The graph doesn’t support any of the other statements, so C is the best answer.

topics.title: Words to know
topics.content:
**Abundance** — how much there is or how many there are of something

**Climate** — long–term weather patterns and average temperatures

**Community** — all of the interacting organisms in an area

**Competition** — type of interaction in which one organism gains a resource at the expense of another

**Cooperation** — type of interaction in which organisms both benefit

**Distribution** — area or areas where an organism is found

**Diversity** — variety of species found in a place

**Ecosystem** — set of living and nonliving things that function together

**Environment** — everything surrounding us

**Habitat** — place an organism lives

**Interact** — affect, connect with, or do things with other organisms

**Pollution** — spoiling resources, such as water, land, and air, by making them dirty or poisonous

**Population** — group of organisms of the same species in a big or small area

topics.title: Video: What Do Ecologists Study?
topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

What do Ecologists study? Scientists that study ecology are called ecologists. Ecologists study several things: Diversity is the variety of life found on Earth. To describe the diversity of your local park, you would list the birds, trees, flowers, and insects you see there. Distribution is all the places a species lives. For example, the pale rose finch lives in Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and Israel. Abundance is how many there are of a species. The abundance of pale rose finches in Jordan is about 10,000. The environment is everything around us. It can mean the city where you live, the air you breathe, and the rocky surface of our planet, Earth. Interaction is how living things affect other living things and connect to their environment. Organizing the world In ecology, scientists organize the world into big regions and smaller areas or groups within them. The biosphere includes everything on Earth and the atmosphere that surrounds it. Biomes are regions of the world with similar climates, animals, and plants – for example, a dessert Ecosystems are sets of living and nonliving things that function together – for example, the trees, animals, and rivers in a rainforest A community is all of the organisms (living things) in an area – for example, all the fish, birds, insects, and plants that live around a small pond. A population is a separate group of organisms in one species – for example, the deer that live on one side of a mountain range that never mingles with the deer population on the other side. This map shows the world’s biomes. Courtesy of Ville Koistinen. ■ Check for understanding Use the information in the map of the world’s biomes above to answer the question. Southern Asia and southeastern North America are circled on the map. The dark green areas that are circled represent tropical rainforest biomes. Which other areas on the map show tropical rainforest biomes? a. North Africa and Saudi Arabia show tropical rainforest biomes. b. North Africa and Northern Mexico show tropical rainforest biomes. c. Northwestern South America and Central Africa show tropical rainforest biomes. d. Central Europe and western North America show tropical rainforest biomes. Explanation and Answers: Looking at the map, we can see that other dark green areas including Northwestern South America and

Central Africa show tropical rainforest biomes. So those areas also show tropical rainforest biomes.

topics.title: Organisms and their habitats
topics.content:
The place where an organism lives is called its habitat .

A habitat provides the things an organism needs to survive. Organisms need the right climate and amount of water. They also need other organisms.

A large fish, Epinephelus tukula, is cleaned by two cleaner fish. Image courtesy of Richard Ling.

So, what affects how many organisms can live in a place?

No living thing can live without other living things. All organisms interact with others to survive. Let’s look at some interactions in the natural world:

• Resources are the things all organisms need to survive. They include water and maybe shelter. But resources also include other organisms, such as members of their own species to mate with. Resources are also the species of animals and plants they eat.

• Many interactions happen when organisms are looking for food. The organisms that hunt and eat other organisms are called predators. The organisms that are being hunted are called prey.

• In a competition, something wins and something loses. For example, if a wolf and a bear are both trying to eat a dead deer, they are competing for food.

• Organisms also interact through cooperation. For example, “cleaner fish” are small fish that clean parasites off larger fish. The large fish could easily eat the cleaner fish, but they do not. The fish are working together, or cooperating – the cleaner fish get food when they eat the parasites; the larger fish get rid of the parasites. This is a win–win interaction!

topics.title: People and Ecology
topics.content:
Humans change the environment all the time. If you have completed the social studies class, you will have learned about people and the environment. Now let’s look at how people affect ecology.

• Human activity has changed Earth’s environment with buildings, agriculture, and industry. Over 40 percent of land is now farmed. Fewer organisms can live in farmed regions because the ecosystems have changed.

• Humans use a lot of fresh water. They build dams to keep the water where they want to use it. They change rivers to move water closer to cities. When people use fresh water, it isn’t always available for other organisms.

• People also cause a lot of pollution. Trash, chemicals, and other pollutants get into the water and land. They harm other organisms and ecosystems.

• Farming, industry, and processes that produce energy all release gasses into the air. Carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, and methane are gasses that trap heat from the Sun in Earth’s atmosphere. More and more of these gasses are warming the planet and changing the world’s climate. Climate change leads to other changes, including the extinction of species.

topics.title: Words to know
topics.content:
**Consumer** — an organism that gets its food energy from other organisms

**Ecosystem Service** — a process of an ecosystem that benefits people

**Energy** — power or food that organisms use to survive

**Erosion** — slow destruction of surfaces, such as soil or rock, by wind or water

**Food Web-connected** — ways that energy moves through an ecosystem from one organism to another

**Keystone Species** — species that play the most important role in the way an ecosystem functions

topics.title: Types of Ecosystems
topics.content:
An ecosystem is a dynamic network of living organisms—such as plants, animals, and microorganisms—interacting with one another and their physical environment, which includes nonliving elements like soil, water, and climate. These interactions create a complex web of relationships that support life and maintain ecological balance.

The Earth is home to a diverse array of ecosystems, both large and small, each uniquely adapted to its specific environment. These ecosystems do not exist in isolation; they interact with and influence one another, contributing to the planet's overall health and stability.

Examples of various kinds of ecosystems, or Biomes

Producers and consumers

Ecologists divide organisms into producers and consumers. Producers and consumers get their energy to live and grow in different ways.

Producers are organisms that make their own energy or food. Plants are an example of producers because they make food from the Sun’s energy, through a process called photosynthesis.

Consumers are organisms that receive energy from other organisms. A rabbit that eats a plant, or a fox that eats a rabbit, are consumers.

topics.title: Food Chains
topics.content:
A simple food chain

Rabbit eats grass. Fox eats rabbit.

When a rabbit eats a plant and a fox eats a rabbit, the process is called a food chain. It is a chain because one thing leads to another. But not all energy in an ecosystem moves in such direct chains. Sometimes, it is more like a web of connections.

The different ways that energy moves through an ecosystem from one organism to another is called a food web . A food web shows the many ways that plants and animals are connected and share energy. A good web may contain several food chains.

The image above is an example of a marine food web.

topics.title: Ecosystem Services and Keystone Species
topics.content:
Ecosystems provide many valuable services that benefit humans. Here are some examples of these services:

• Bacteria that help purify water.

• Tree roots that prevent soil erosion.

• Bees that pollinate plants.

• Oceans that provide fish for food.

These important contributions from nature are known as ecosystem services . They result from the interactions between living organisms and their environment. Among the most essential services we receive from ecosystems are food and clean water.

What Keeps Ecosystems Healthy?

Ecosystems tend to remain stable if left undisturbed by humans. Every part of an ecosystem plays a role in keeping it functioning well. However, some species are especially crucial. These species are called keystone species .

The American Beaver  is one example of a keystone species in North America. Photograph Via NatGeo

When a keystone species declines in number or disappears, it can have significant effects on the entire ecosystem. For example, the loss of a keystone species can lead to changes in plant and animal populations, disrupting the balance of the ecosystem. Understanding the importance of these species helps us appreciate the interconnectedness of nature and the services it provides.

topics.title: Video: How the Ecosystem Changes
topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Let’s look at a keystone species in the Yellowstone National Park ecosystem and how it affects other species and the environment. Scientists study Yellowstone’s ecosystem because it is mostly untouched by humans. Wolves once lived in Yellowstone, but they were killed off by ranchers for eating their sheep and cattle. In 1995, Yellowstone Park brought back wolves. For 20 years, scientists studied the impact of this on the ecosystem. As predators, the wolves killed and ate the elk, so they helped control the elk population. The danger from wolves made elk hide in the forested mountains. But when wolves were not present, elk grazed in the fertile river valleys. The elk would eat the willow trees along the river banks. When the wolves came back, the elk went back to the forests, and the willow trees grew back. As more trees grew, the willows’ roots helped keep the riverbanks strong, and now there is less erosion from soil washing away. The growth of trees along the river had other impacts. Because trees provide a habitat for small songbirds, the population of songbirds in the park increased. Beavers use trees to build dams or structures that cause water to pool. When wolves are present, the beaver population increases. Why? Because there are more trees for the beavers to use in their dams! All these things happened because wolves were reintroduced into Yellowstone National Park. Here is a diagram that shows the effects. When we look at all these details, we can understand why wolves are called a Keystone Species in Yellowstone National Park. The wolves had a lot of impact on other species in the ecosystem. When the wolves were brought back to the park, the Elk population was controlled. The elks stayed in the forest, instead of by the river. So, more trees grew. The tree roots slowed erosion. Songbirds lived in the trees, so the Songbirds population increased. Beavers used the trees to build dams, so the beaver population increased.

How old is Earth?
Shortly after radioactivity was discovered in 1896, scientists realized they could figure out how old rock was by measuring how much of the uranium in it had decayed into lead. This process is called radiometric dating.
When a rock is formed in the bowels of the planet, uranium atoms are trapped within it. These atoms will decay as the rock ages. Radiometric dating measures the ratio of radioactive isotopes within the rock. From this, scientists can figure out how long it has been around.
In 1913, geologist Arthur Holmes published “The Age of the Earth,” the first major effort to date the planet using radiometric dating.

topics.title: Layers of Earth
topics.content:
Geology is a branch of Earth Science that deals with the Earth's physical structure, how it formed, and how it changes. Geologists are scientists who study the Earth and the matter on Earth.

Layers of Earth

Geologists study Earth’s rocky layers: how the layers formed and how they continue to change. Although we only see the surface, there’s a lot going on under the ground.

The layers of Earth from the surface (crust) to the core.

The planet Earth has four main layers. Starting deep in the center:

• In the middle of Earth is the inner core . It is solid, made of iron and nickel, and very, very hot.

• Surrounding the inner core is the outer core. The outer core is made of liquid iron and nickel.

• Next is the mantle. It is the widest layer and is made of a hot melted rock called magma .

• The top, outside layer is the crust. The surface rocks are hard. The crust is the surface of Earth that we live on. Mountains, deserts, oceans, forests, and all of life are on Earth’s crust.

topics.title: Tectonic Plates
topics.content:
Earth’s crust is broken up into tectonic plates . These plates are separate pieces that fit together to form Earth’s surface layer. These plates are huge, bigger than continents. The plates float on the magma below, moving gradually over thousands or millions of years.

This map shows Earth’s tectonic plates. You can see the United States is on the North American Plate.

Types of Tectonic Plate Boundaries

Tectonic plates have three main types of boundaries (edges) that reflect the different ways they move. The three types are:

• Divergent boundaries: where plates are moving away from each other

• Convergent boundaries: where plates move towards each other and meet

• Transform boundaries: where plates slide along beside each other

Source: geographicbook.com

Most seismic activity occurs at three types of plate boundaries. The San Andreas fault is an example of a famous transform boundary tectonic plate along with the Pacific plate.

GED Exam Tip: How to Find Supporting Evidence in a Scientific Text You’ve learned that good scientific theories require supporting evidence. Your test will ask you to find supporting evidence for scientific claims or theories. This test tip will show you how to identify supporting evidence. Let’s use a famous theory about how continents formed. Read the text and choose the best answer to the question below. Wegener's Theory (adapted from “Dive and Discover”) Geologists believed Earth formed 4.6 billion years ago. Until recently, they thought that the oceans and continents were always where they are now. But less than 100 years ago, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener noticed similar plant and animal fossils were found in both Africa and South America and on other continents separated by oceans. Similar rock formations were also found on distant continents. This suggested that the formations were once whole and later divided. Wegener also noticed that if you pushed Western Europe and Africa together with North and South America, their coastlines would fit together very neatly. Wegener developed a theory that the continents were once connected but had separated and drifted apart. Which of the statements from the text support Wegener’s theory that Earth’s continents were once connected? Choose the best answer. A. Earth formed 4.6 billion years ago. B. Similar plant and animal fossils were found in both Africa and South America and on other continents separated by oceans. Similar rock formations were also found on distant

continents. C. If you pushed Western Europe and Africa together with North and South America, their coastlines would fit together very neatly. D. Both B and C. To answer this question, you will use the same process you always use for multiple-choice questions: you will make sure you understand the question, and you will check the statements against the data to find the best answer. But when you look for supporting evidence, you only need to ask yourself one question: does it support the claim, theory, or prediction? For example, (A) may be true, but it does not support a theory about how continents formed. (B) and (C), however, both support the idea that continents were once joined. You could choose either of those. But (D) is even better because it includes both sets of evidence. So the best answer is (D). You may see combined choices like “Both B and C” in your test. The last choice in the list may also say something like “None of the above” or “All of the above.” You will still need to test all the statements! Another note: you may also need to find supporting evidence in diagrams. You can use the same approach.

topics.title: Fossils and Minerals
topics.content:
Fossils

Another important part of geology is the study of fossils. Fossils have taught scientists much of what they know about life before humans. Fossils are pieces or imprints (like a footprint) of animals, plants, or other organisms that have been preserved from a long time ago. People often find fossils that are millions of years old.

An AI generated image of a dinosaur fossil

The fossils show where and when different plants and animals lived. Many of the species are extinct, and no longer exist. Some examples of fossils are dinosaur bones and imprints of the shells of sea creatures from millions of years ago and can be found most often in sedimentary rocks.

Minerals

Geologists study minerals, too. A mineral is a nonliving substance that occurs naturally on Earth.

Minerals are everywhere, including in food! Salt, for example, is a mineral. Minerals combine to make other substances. We’ll learn more about minerals later in science class.
