topics.title: Atmosphere and Air Pressure
topics.content:
The Earth's atmosphere is divided into different parts, as shown in the image above

The Earth's Atmosphere: A Vital Shield

The atmosphere is the layer of gases that surrounds our planet, Earth. It plays a crucial role in supporting life, protecting us from harmful space elements, and regulating temperatures. Without the atmosphere, life as we know it would not exist.

Composition of the Atmosphere

The atmosphere is made up of a mixture of gases, which include:

• 78% Nitrogen (N■): The most abundant gas in the atmosphere. While nitrogen itself is not involved in the breathing process, it helps maintain the balance of gases in the air.

• 21% Oxygen (O■): Essential for respiration in humans and animals, oxygen allows us to breathe and provides the fuel our cells need to produce energy.

• 0.93% Argon (Ar): An inert gas, meaning it doesn't react with other substances easily. Though present in small amounts, argon plays a role in filling the gaps between other gases.

• 0.039% Carbon Dioxide (CO■): Though present in small quantities, carbon dioxide is vital for plant life, which absorbs it during photosynthesis. Additionally, CO■ helps regulate Earth's temperature by trapping some of the Sun's heat.

• 0.4–1% Water Vapor (H■O): The amount of water vapor varies depending on weather conditions. Water vapor is important for the water cycle and helps form clouds, rain, and snow.

• Trace amounts of other gases: This includes methane (CH■), nitrous oxide (N■O), ozone (O■), neon (Ne), helium (He), krypton (Kr), and hydrogen (H■). Though these gases make up less than 1% of the atmosphere, some, like ozone, have critical functions.

Layers of the Atmosphere

The Earth's atmosphere is divided into five distinct layers, each with unique characteristics:

• Troposphere: This is the lowest layer, where we live and where weather occurs. The troposphere extends up to about 8 to 15 kilometers (5 to 9 miles) above sea level.

• Stratosphere: Above the troposphere is the stratosphere, where the ozone layer is found. The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays, protecting life on Earth.

• Mesosphere: This is the middle layer, where meteors burn up as they enter Earth's atmosphere.

• Thermosphere: The thermosphere is characterized by high temperatures and contains the ionosphere, which is important for radio communications and auroras (like the Northern Lights).

• Exosphere: The outermost layer, where the atmosphere gradually fades into space. This is where satellites orbit the Earth.

Importance of the Atmosphere

• Breathing and Life Support: The atmosphere provides the oxygen we breathe and helps regulate the gases needed for various biological processes. Without it, life could not survive.

• Temperature Regulation: The atmosphere acts as a blanket, trapping heat from the Sun and preventing the Earth from becoming too cold at night. This process is known as the greenhouse effect.

• Protection from UV Radiation: The ozone layer within the stratosphere absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun, protecting humans and animals from skin cancer and other damage caused by UV rays.

• Weather and Climate: The atmosphere is responsible for the Earth's weather and climate systems. It drives wind patterns, precipitation, and the formation of storms.

topics.title: What is Air Pressure
topics.content:
The atmosphere is made of molecules or tiny particles of substances. Molecules are too small to see, but they have weight and movement. The molecules’ weight and movement cause atmospheric pressure – what

people call air pressure.

When you press a hand pump, it pushes the air within the tube, which moves and creates pressure that makes the needle move. When you release the pump, the pressure of air on the needle decreases and it moves back

Pressure is the weight of something pushing down. Where air molecules are close together, the air is heavier, and air pressure is high. Air molecules are more spread out higher up in the atmosphere. There, the air is lighter, and air pressure goes down.

topics.title: Weather and Meteorology
topics.content:
Changes in pressure affect the world’s weather. As you know, the weather changes all the time. Changes are caused by changing conditions in the lower atmosphere. Weather conditions include rain and snow, wind, low and high pressure, storminess, cloudiness, and fluctuations in temperature.

Weather is happening outside daily. This forecast shows the weather for a week.

Meteorology is a branch of Earth science focused on the study of the atmosphere and weather patterns. Scientists who specialize in predicting and studying the weather are known as meteorologists . These experts monitor and analyze the movement of weather systems across the globe using advanced tools such as satellite imagery, radar, and computer models. Meteorologists can provide forecasts that predict whether it will be sunny, rainy, or stormy today, tomorrow, or even several days in advance.

The climate of an area is determined by the average weather patterns taken over a long period of time. Understanding a region’s climate helps us to know what type of weather we can expect.

topics.title: Ocean Currents
topics.content:
Ocean currents are primarily driven by wind patterns and variations in water temperature. These currents play a crucial role in transferring heat across the oceans, moving warm water from the equator toward the poles and bringing cooler water from the poles back toward the equator. This heat exchange significantly influences global weather and climate by redistributing thermal energy and impacting atmospheric conditions.

Understanding Climate Patterns

The map presented above shows average temperatures (°F) from October 1981 to 2010, illustrating typical climate patterns across the mainland United States. This climate map uses temperature data collected over several decades to reveal general trends and variations.

In this map, a color code highlights the average October temperatures, showcasing the stark contrasts between different regions. For example, the northern and northwestern United States exhibit cooler temperatures compared to the warmer conditions found in the southern and southeastern regions. Such disparities in climate are directly related to the uneven heating of the Earth, which is further influenced by ocean currents and their interaction with atmospheric systems. Understanding these patterns is essential for comprehending the broader implications of climate variability on ecosystems and human activities.

Eratosthenes
Early scientists believed their world was probably a sphere, the shape of a ball. But they did not know the size of Earth until about 240 BCE when Eratosthenes performed a scientific experiment.
Eratosthenes received a letter from a friend in Syene, a city in southern Egypt. In the letter, his friend mentioned that at the time of the summer solstice, the Sun would be directly overhead, and nothing would have a shadow. That is, if you had a completely vertical (straight up and down) object, it would not have a shadow.
But Eratosthenes knew that this wasn’t the case in northern Egypt. At exactly the same time on that same day, vertical objects do have shadows. The Sun’s rays were coming from the same direction as the rays shining on Syene. But the rays were hitting Earth at a different angle.
Eratosthenes was a scientist, so he did an experiment. He measured the length of the shadow cast by a vertical stick at noon on the day of the summer solstice. From the length, he figured out the angle of the Sun in relation to the vertical stick placed at Alexandria, the city he lived in. The angle measured one-fiftieth of a circle or 7.2 degrees.
Eratosthenes also measured the distance between the two cities. With the angle and the distance, Eratosthenes was able to calculate the curve in Earth’s surface. He used that to figure out the circumference (the distance around). His calculations were amazingly accurate, even using such simple scientific methods.

Eratosthenes
Early scientists believed their world was probably a sphere, the shape of a ball. But they did not know the size of Earth until about 240 BCE when Eratosthenes performed a scientific experiment.
Eratosthenes received a letter from a friend in Syene, a city in southern Egypt. In the letter, his friend mentioned that at the time of the summer solstice, the Sun would be directly overhead, and nothing would have a shadow. That is, if you had a completely vertical (straight up and down) object, it would not have a shadow.
But Eratosthenes knew that this wasn’t the case in northern Egypt. At exactly the same time on that same day, vertical objects do have shadows. The Sun’s rays were coming from the same direction as the rays shining on Syene. But the rays were hitting Earth at a different angle.
Eratosthenes was a scientist, so he did an experiment. He measured the length of the shadow cast by a vertical stick at noon on the day of the summer solstice. From the length, he figured out the angle of the Sun in relation to the vertical stick placed at Alexandria, the city he lived in. The angle measured one-fiftieth of a circle or 7.2 degrees.
Eratosthenes also measured the distance between the two cities. With the angle and the distance, Eratosthenes was able to calculate the curve in Earth’s surface. He used that to figure out the circumference (the distance around). His calculations were amazingly accurate, even using such simple scientific methods.
QUESTION: What did Eratosthenes calculate that enabled him to figure out Earth’s circumference?

Explanation:

So, while both

questions.prompt: Which planet in our solar system is known for having a prominent ring system?
questions.explanation:
Answer:
c) Saturn
Explanation:
Saturn is famous for its stunning ring system, which is the most extensive and complex in our solar system. While other planets like Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have ring systems, Saturn’s rings are the most prominent and easily visible from Earth through a small telescope. These rings are primarily composed of ice particles, with some dust and rock, and they span a vast area around the planet, making Saturn one of the most recognizable and iconic planets in our solar system. Mars, on the other hand, does not have rings, and while Jupiter and Neptune have rings, they are much fainter and less prominent than Saturn’s.

topics.title: Where is Earth
topics.content:
Earth revolving around the sun

Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun, which is the center of our solar system.

The term "solar" refers to anything related to the Sun, so when we talk about our group of planets, we call it the solar system . The solar system is vast, yet it represents only a small part of a much larger structure called a galaxy, which contains many other solar systems.

Our galaxy is known as the Milky Way . The Milky Way is just one of countless galaxies in the universe. The universe encompasses everything that exists, including all galaxies, stars, planets, and other celestial bodies. In fact, there are billions of galaxies in the universe! Some of the bright stars we see in the night sky are actually suns from distant solar systems, each potentially hosting their own planets.

Understanding this cosmic structure helps us appreciate the vastness of the universe and our small yet significant place within it.

topics.title: Our Solar System
topics.content:
The solar system is made up of the Sun, eight planets, their moons, asteroids, comets, and other celestial objects. At the center of our solar system is the Sun, a massive ball of fire that provides the light and heat necessary for life on Earth.

Surrounding the Sun are the eight planets, which you should be familiar with, as their names may come up in your studies. These planets vary in size, composition, and distance from the Sun.

The image below illustrates the eight planets of our solar system, showcasing their unique characteristics and positions relative to the Sun. Understanding this structure helps us grasp the complexity and beauty of our cosmic neighborhood.

A diagram of the Sun (on the left side of the image) and planets in our solar system shows their relative sizes. You can see that Earth is one of the smallest planets. Image: “Planets2013” courtesy of WP, Creative Commons.

In addition to the planets, there are smaller objects like dwarf planets and moons. Just as the planets orbit the Sun, moons orbit their respective planets. For example, Earth has one moon, while other planets, like Jupiter and Saturn, have many moons.

topics.title: Looking at Space
topics.content:
How do we know what is in space?

We know because of the science of astronomy . For thousands of years, before the invention of telescopes, astronomers simply observed space from Earth. By looking at the Sun, the planets, and the movement of stars, astronomers developed theories about the universe and about Earth. They made mathematical calculations to do so. The invention of the first telescopes helped to prove or disprove early theories.

Courtesy: TheFactSite.Com

Today, we have powerful telescopes in space that send images back to Earth. They allow us to see solar systems far beyond our own. Because of telescopes, our knowledge of space has grown and changed.

topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Earth is considered one of the inner planets along with Venus and Mars, because they are relatively close to the Sun. Earth has about 70% of its surface covered by water. It is considered the only Celestial body in the solar system on which life is known to exist. Earth's moon is the fifth-largest in the solar system. The moon itself has no atmosphere, but it does have some surface ice, discovered in 1998. The moon revolves around the Earth once every 27 days. Earth’s tilt creates seasons Earth is tilted (leaning) at a small angle in relation to the Sun while it orbits. The part of Earth tilted toward the Sun gets more sunlight and is warmer. The part tilted away from the Sun is colder because it receives less sunlight. As Earth orbits the Sun over one year, different parts tilt away and toward the Sun at different times. This tilt is why Earth has seasons every year. The summer season is in the part of the world tilted toward the sun. The part tilted away experiences winter. Want to explore more with Space Science visit Bill Nye The Science Guy Earth’s rotation creates day and night As Earth travels around the Sun, it is spinning. This is called rotating (turning) on its own axis . The axis is like an imaginary stick through the middle of a spinning ball. Earth’s axis runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. As Earth spins on its axis, the part turns towards the Sun’s light experiences day. As it spins away, the day becomes night. Image courtesy of tes.com As Earth spins, different parts face the Sun and have their daytime. When these same places turn away from the Sun, it gets dark and they have nighttime. It takes Earth 24 hours to make one full rotation (turn). The regions of the world constantly move from day to night in this 24–hour cycle. Why the moon seems to change Earth’s moon orbits Earth in the same way that Earth orbits the Sun. That is why we see the moon rise and set. The light that we see coming from the moon is sunlight reflecting off the moon’s surface. Sometimes just a small slice of the moon is lit up, and sometimes the whole side appears to be shining – what we call a full moon.

topics.title: Parts of Atoms
topics.content:
Everything living and non–living is made of matter. This includes you and the air around you! Matter can be made of one thing or a mix of things.  Matter is composed of tiny parts called atoms, known as the smallest unit of matter.  Atoms are the “building blocks” for everything else.  Each element has its own type of atom that makes it what it is. Like the nucleus of a cell, the nucleus of an atom decides what the atom is. But atoms are made of subatomic particles and are thousands of times smaller than cells!

There are three parts to an atom you need to know about:

• The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons.

• The electrons move around the nucleus, like planets orbiting the Sun

• The atomic mass of an atom is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons that it contains.

This diagram of a calcium atom shows the nucleus at the center surrounded by electrons. The calcium atom has 20 electrons, 20 protons, and 20 neutrons. The number of protons (20) is what makes this atom calcium. To calculate the atomic mass, add the numbers of protons and neutrons together.  Image courtesy of the Atomic Age.

topics.title: Positive and Negative Charges
topics.content:
Protons and neutrons are attracted (pulled together) by a force called an electrical charge . A charge is the amount of electricity in an object. For your test, you will need to know:

• Electrons are particles with a negative (minus or –) charge of 1.

• Protons are particles with a positive (plus or +) charge of 1.

• Neutrons are particles with no charge: they are neutral.

• Ions are groups of atoms with a positive or negative charge.

• The opposite charges are attracted to each other, and this force is one of the things that hold the atom together.

Atoms start with the same number of electrons and protons, so they have zero electrical charge. But sometimes they lose or gain electrons. When the number of electrons is not the same as the number of protons, the charge is no longer zero, and the atom becomes charged. A charged atom (one with an electric charge) is called an ion.

If there are more electrons, the atom is negatively charged. It becomes an anion. But if there are more protons, then the atom is positively charged. This type of atom is a cation.

This diagram shows a helium atom as positive (a cation), neutral, and negative (an anion).

Electrons are shown with – , protons are shown with + , and neutrons are green.

Atoms have no charge when there are the same number of electrons and protons. When there are more protons or electrons, the atom acquires a charge and is an ion.

topics.title: GED Exam Tip
topics.content:
Exam tip You may get a question about the charges in an atom. To prepare for these questions, look at a diagram of an atom and memorize these facts about atoms and their charges: Each electron has a negative charge of 1. Each proton has a positive charge of 1. Neutrons have no charge. A charged atom is called an ion. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons. The atomic mass of an atom is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons. If you understand and remember these facts, you can apply them to answer these questions. You will also do some simple adding and subtracting. Here are a couple of example questions to show how we apply the facts. If you memorize the basic facts, you will be able to answer questions about atoms and their charges. The math will be simple once you know which numbers to use. For example: An ion has 12 protons and 14 neutrons. This ion will have an overall positive charge if its number of electrons equals what? To get the correct answer, apply the facts. Protons have a

positive charge. So, for the ion to have a positive charge, it must have fewer electrons than protons. 11 is fewer than 12, so the answer is 11.

topics.title: Video: Elements and Molecules
topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Elements Scientists have discovered and named only 118 different types of atoms. When atoms of one kind group together, they make elements. Elements are matter with only one kind of atom and are substances that cannot be broken. Hydrogen and oxygen are elements. So are gold and carbon. Each element has a chemical symbol. Hydrogen, H, and Gold, Au; for example. Each element’s atom has a different number of protons from any other element’s atom. That number is anywhere from 1 to 118 because there are 118 known types of atoms. As we saw in the diagram of a calcium atom above, the number of protons (20) is what makes that atom a calcium atom. It’s the same for all the other atoms in elements, from gold (79 protons) to oxygen (8 protons). The number of protons tells the element what to be and tells us what it is! What is a substance in science? You hear people talking about substances in everyday English. For example, they may say glue is a sticky substance. But in science, substance means matter made of specific atoms. Elements are one kind of substance. If two different elements join together, you get a new substance in definite proportions, this is called a compound. Water is a great example of a compound. At room temperature water is a liquid, however separately, Hydrogen and Oxygen are gasses. A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances that keep their own properties; like saltwater. Molecules and compounds This is a diagram of a water molecule. Water molecules have one oxygen (O) atom and two hydrogen (H) atoms. We learned that every atom is a tiny piece of matter. We learned that atoms of one kind group together to form elements. When atoms join together, they form a molecule. A molecule with two or more atoms is held together with bonds. Oxygen, for example, is made of oxygen molecules, which are oxygen atoms bonded together. When atoms or molecules of different elements join together, they become a compound. All substances on the earth except elements are compounds. For example, one atom of oxygen combined with two atoms of hydrogen makes the compound we call water. How do molecules join together? To join together, molecules make chemical bonds. Chemical bonds are like glue. They join atoms together to form molecules and they join molecules together to make compounds. There are two main kinds of chemical bonds you will need to recognize. Ionic bonds form when a metal joins with a nonmetal. Ionic bonds will gain or lose electrons to become ions that attract ions to hold the compound together; like table salt. Covalent bonds form when two non–metallic ions join together. In covalent bonds, atoms will share a pair of electrons; one electron each; like water. In the next lesson, we’ll learn what makes substances join and change.

topics.title: Physical Changes
topics.content:
In science, we learn that molecules (the building blocks of matter) can bond together to form various substances. These substances can change their form or "state" based on temperature and other conditions.

The four main states of matter you'll need to know for your GED test are solids , liquids , gases , and plasma .

• Solids : In solids, the molecules are packed tightly together, which is why solids keep their shape. For example, a rock , wood , or a desk stays the same shape unless you forcefully break it.

• Liquids : In liquids, the molecules are more loosely packed, allowing them to flow and take the shape of their container. Think about water , juice , or oil —they can be poured, and they’ll fill up the bottom of whatever container they’re in.

• Gases : In gases, the molecules are spread out and move freely. This is why gases don’t have a definite shape and can expand to fill any space. For instance, the air we breathe is made up of gases like oxygen and nitrogen. If you blow up a balloon , the gas inside takes up all the space within the balloon.

• Plasma : Plasma is the fourth state of matter and is different from the other three. In plasma, the gas molecules become electrically charged, or "ionized," because they have so much energy. Plasma is found in very hot places, like the sun and stars , where temperatures are extremely high. You can also find plasma in things like lightning and neon signs . Plasma doesn’t have a fixed shape, like gases, but it behaves differently because of the charged particles.

These changes in state happen when temperature and pressure conditions change. For example, heating a solid like ice turns it into liquid water, and heating water turns it into steam (gas). If you heat gas to extremely high temperatures, it becomes plasma.

Ice melts to make water and water evaporates to form gases. This is one example of a matter changing its state

The pictures above show water in all three states of matter, or phases : ice (solid), water (liquid), and steam (gas). Both gasses and liquids are fluids , which means they can change shape according to where they are.

• Gasses are like air. In a gas, there is a lot of space between the molecules. Gasses have a lot of volume when they are not contained because they can spread out. They have no definite shape and no definite volume.

• Liquids are like milk. They have less space between molecules. They can change shape. They have definite volume but not shape.

• Solids are like wood. They have very little space in between the molecules. They have a more fixed shape. They have definite shape and volume.

Substances can melt from solid to liquid and they can boil from liquid to gas. The changes can go in the other direction too.

Condensing is what happens when a gas changes to a liquid. For example, water vapor turning into rain drops.

Freezing is a process that changes a liquid into a solid, like freezing water to become ice.

In these physical changes, atoms and molecules move from one state to another. But the substance stayed the same. Water is still water when it is ice or steam. That’s because it still has the same molecules made of hydrogen and oxygen.

topics.title: Chemical Changes
topics.content:
A chemical change happens when the substance changes into a different substance. The process that causes this is called a chemical reaction . In a chemical reaction, the atoms or ions of one or more reactants are rearranged, yielding one or more products. Chemical reactions can be represented by formulas and are either endothermic or exothermic. Mass is conserved during chemical reactions. Chemical reactions are happening around us all the time. They are essential for life on Earth.  Chemical changes caused by chemical reactions happen in science and in everyday life.

What happens in a chemical reaction?

Chemical reactions cause molecules to form bonds or break bonds. That’s how new substances are made. Here are some everyday chemical reactions:

• Two substances mix together

• One substance separates into two

• Something burns

• Something gives off a gas

• Something rusts

• Things change into something else, like when you bake a cake!

topics.title: Reactants and Products
topics.content:
In a chemical reaction, we start with reactants —these are the substances that take part in the reaction. After the reaction happens, we get products , which are the new substances that are created.

Even though the products look different from the reactants, the atoms don’t disappear or get destroyed. Instead, they get rearranged to form new substances. This is a key idea in chemistry: matter is never lost or created in a chemical reaction; it just changes form.

This diagram shows what happens to atoms or molecules during four different types of chemical reactions. The reactants are to the left of the arrows. The products are to the right of the arrows. Note that none of the atoms went away in the reaction. They just rearranged themselves.

Many chemical reactions fall into one of the types of reaction in the diagram above. Let’s apply the reactions to processes in real life:

• Synthesis or combination: Two substances combine to make one new substance. Example : A simple everyday example is rust forming on a nail. When iron (Fe) in the nail combines with oxygen (O■) in the air, they form a new substance called iron oxide (Fe■O■), or rust.

• Decomposition : One substance turns into two new ones. Example : Heating up sugar is a decomposition reaction. When you heat sugar in a pan, it breaks down into carbon (which turns it black) and water vapor, causing it to caramelize or burn.

• Single Displacement (exchange): A molecule or atom from one substance switches to another substance. Example : Cleaning tarnished silver with aluminum foil and baking soda is a single displacement reaction. The aluminum (Al) takes the tarnish (sulfur) off the silver (Ag), making it shiny again.

• Double Displacement (exchange): One molecule or atom from each substance switches to the other substance. Example : Mixing baking soda with vinegar is a classic example of double displacement. When you mix baking soda and vinegar, they swap parts and form carbon dioxide (CO■), which creates bubbles.

topics.title: Combustion and Catalysts
topics.content:
Another important reaction is combustion.

Combustion is what happens when wood burns. A reactant , usually one that contains carbon, combines with oxygen, usually from the air, and releases energy. A catalyst is anything that helps a chemical reaction occur or speeds it up. Adding gasoline to a fire is a catalyst because it makes the fire burst into flames.

Burning of wood is combustion

Let's look at an example:

When wood burns in a combustion process, the reactants and catalysts involved are as follows:

Reactants

• Wood : The primary reactant, which is composed mainly of cellulose (C6H10O5), hemicellulose, and lignin.

• Oxygen (O2) : From the air, it reacts with the components of wood to produce heat, light, carbon dioxide, and water.

Catalysts

In the combustion process of wood, catalysts are not typically used. However, certain conditions or substances can facilitate the combustion process:

• Heat : While not a catalyst in the traditional sense, heat is necessary to initiate the combustion process by breaking down the wood's complex molecules into simpler forms that can react with oxygen.

• Charcoal or Ash : In some cases, residual charcoal or ash from previous burns can act to maintain and spread the heat within the fire, although they do not serve as true catalysts.

In most cases, combustion needs an external heat source to start the reaction.

Exothermic and Endothermic Reaction

Energy is involved in all chemical reactions. A reaction in which the reactants absorb energy from their surroundings is an endothermic reaction. For example, a scrambled egg solidifies when you add heat (energy) to it.

A reaction in which energy is given off with the products, usually in the form of heat or light, is an exothermic reaction. When you burn wood in a fireplace, for example, heat and light energy or giving off activation energy is the amount of energy needed to get the reactions going.

topics.content:

Each element has its own symbol of one or two letters. It’s like the letters we use for states in the United States: TX for Texas, for example. In this case, it’s Ti for Titanium!

You will probably remember that each element’s atom has its own special number of protons. That number gives the element its atomic number in the table, from 1 to 118.

topics.title: Chemical Formulas
topics.content:
A chemical formula is a way to show what a substance is made of using symbols and numbers. Each symbol represents an element (a basic type of matter), and the numbers show how many atoms of each element are in the substance.

Think of it like a recipe that tells you which ingredients (elements) are in a substance and how much of each is needed!

For example:

• Water has the formula H■O . This means each water molecule is made of 2 hydrogen (H) atoms and 1 oxygen (O) atom.

Oxygen’s symbol is O , and hydrogen’s symbol is H . The formula for water is H 2 O because water molecules are made of two hydrogens (H) and one oxygen (O) element. This diagram shows the chemical formula for water.

topics.title: Understanding Subscripts
topics.content:
H■O

As we just learnt, H 2 O is the chemical formula of water.

What is the “little” 2 written immediately after the element symbol (H) ?

This number written low on the line is called a subscript . In a chemical formula, the subscript tells you the number of atoms of an element that a molecule has.

A subscript of “2” means that 2 atoms of that element are in that molecule. For two hydrogen atoms, we do not write HH. We write H 2 . Water has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So it is written H 2 O, as in the diagram here. The O does not have a little number after it. That tells us there is only one oxygen atom. The formula for carbon dioxide is CO 2 . That’s one carbon and two oxygen atoms.

This is a methane molecule, as seen in the diagram, that has 4 hydrogen atoms bonded with one carbon atom.

Here is another example. To show that something has four atoms of hydrogen, scientists write H 4 instead of HHHH. This diagram is a methane molecule. Methane’s chemical formula is CH 4 . The chemical formula tells us what it is made of: one atom of carbon (C) and four atoms of hydrogen (H 4 ).

topics.title: Understanding Coefficients
topics.content:
Sometimes there is a number written before an element in a formula. For example, in the following formulas:

2CO 2 , 6H 2 O , or 4Fe 2 O 3 .

The number written before an element is a coefficient . The coefficient shows how many of the molecules are combined to make that particular substance.

In 2CO 2 , there are two units of CO 2 molecules. In 6H 2 O, there are six H 2 O molecules, and in 4Fe 2 O 3 , there are four Fe 2 O 3 molecules. If there is no coefficient before a formula, it means there is only one unit.

In this equation:

• The Reactants are Hydrogen gas (H■) and oxygen gas (O■).

• The product is Water (H■O).

• Coefficients: A coefficient of "2" is placed in front of H■ and H■O to balance the number of hydrogen atoms on both sides of the equation. A coefficient of "2" is placed in front of H■O to balance the number of oxygen atoms on both sides of the equation.

• Subscripts: The subscript "2" after H in H■ indicates there are two hydrogen atoms in each molecule of hydrogen gas. The subscript "2" after H■O indicates there are two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in each molecule of water.

This balanced equation represents the reaction where hydrogen gas reacts with oxygen gas to form water.

topics.title: What is an Equation?
topics.content:
An equation is a way to show that two things are equal. It has an equal sign (=) in the middle, which means that what is on one side is the same as what is on the other side.

For example:

• In the equation 2 + 3 = 5 , the left side (2 + 3) equals the right side (5). Both sides balance out to the same value.

• Another example is 2y(7) = 14y . Here, the left side (2y times 7) equals the right side (14y).

Think of it like a scale: if you add or change something on one side, you must do the same on the other side to keep it balanced!

Chemical formulas or chemical reactions can also be represented as equations. For example:

H■ + O

→ H■O

This equation tells us that hydrogen combined with oxygen equals water. One side of the equation is H 2 + O. The other side has the same elements and number of elements, but arranged differently: now, they are joined together as H 2 O.

Equations just like this one can show chemical reactions. You will remember from your last lesson that in a chemical reaction, none of the atoms go away. They just change around.

The two sides of this reaction have the same number of each type of atom. They are rearranged and bonded differently after the reaction.

topics.title: Showing Reactions
topics.content:
In a chemical reaction, an arrow (

→) is used instead of an equal sign (=).

The reactants are to the left of the arrows. The products are to the right of the arrows.

All the reactants are still there in the products, although they are rearranged.

You can use chemical equations to show even the most complicated chemical reactions. Here’s a chemical equation that shows a combination reaction:

CO 2 + Na 2 O

→ Na 2 CO 3

This equation tells us that when carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reacts with sodium oxide (Na 2 O), it produces sodium carbonate (Na 2 CO 3 ).

topics.title: What is Motion?
topics.content:
Motion refers to the movement or change in position of a body or object. It's a fundamental concept in physics and something we encounter daily, whether it's a car driving down the street or a person walking across a room.

To understand motion better, we use certain terms to describe and measure it. Two of the most important ways we measure motion are speed and velocity . While these two terms might seem similar, they have key differences. Let’s break them down:

Speed

Speed is the distance an object travels in a certain amount of time. For example, if you walk two miles in one hour, your speed is 2 miles per hour. If you walk 6 kilometers (km) in 3 hours, your speed is still 2 kilometers per hour. This is sometimes written as 2 km/hr.

Velocity

Velocity is similar to speed in that both measure how fast an object moves over a certain distance in a given amount of time. However, the key difference between the two is that velocity includes direction , whereas speed does not. This means that velocity not only tells us how fast an object is moving, but also specifies the direction in which it's moving.

Speed vs. Velocity:

• Speed is simply the rate at which an object covers distance. It is a scalar quantity, meaning it only takes into account the magnitude (how fast something is going) without considering its direction.

• Velocity , on the other hand, is a vector quantity. This means it includes both magnitude (how fast) and direction (where it’s going).

topics.title: Vectors
topics.content:
If the speed or direction is changing, then the velocity also changes. Calculating the velocity of objects is important in physics. Scientists show velocity with arrows called vectors .

The cyclist’s velocity is 15 meters per second (m/s) to the left, shown by the big arrow pointing to the left. But the wind also has a velocity, shown by the small arrows pointing right. It is moving in the opposite direction and more slowly, only 5 m/s to the right.

Velocity, and any other vector, can show movement in more than one direction: south and east, for example, or forward and up. So the vector has two dimensions .

This diagram shows the velocity in two different situations. In (A), the black vector shows the velocity of an arrow shot from the ground. The orange vector shows the horizontal component (heading right) of the velocity, while the blue vector shows the vertical component (going up). In (B), the black vector shows the velocity of a train traveling northeast. The orange vector is the eastward component, and the blue vector is the northward component.

topics.title: Acceleration and Momentum
topics.content:
When you "accelerate" a car, you increase its speed in a direction. Courtesy: Sean Goodwin/Dribble.com

Speed and velocity don’t always stay the same. Things get faster and slower. The name for a change in speed or velocity over time is acceleration .

A note about the word acceleration: in science, acceleration means any change in speed or direction. In everyday life, people use accelerators just for the process of speeding up. They say decelerate to explain the process of slowing down.

Momentum

The amount of motion in a moving object is called momentum. It is easier to understand momentum if you imagine how hard it would be to stop a moving object. A huge rock rolling down a hill is a lot harder to stop than an orange. That’s because it has more momentum.

topics.title: Why do Things Move or Stay Still?
topics.content:
In everyday life, we observe that things move faster, slower, or stop moving altogether. But why does this happen? The answer lies in the concept of force . In physics, force plays a critical role in understanding why objects behave the way they do in motion.

What is Force?

While we often think of "force" as strength or power in daily life, in physics, force is defined as any interaction that causes an object to change its state of motion. It can make an object move, stop, speed up, or slow down.

Pull and Push

Simply put, force is a push or pull that occurs when one object interacts with another.

• For example, when you push a shopping cart, your push is a force that causes the cart to move.

• When a baseball bat hits a ball, the bat exerts a force on the ball, making it fly into the air.

Force and motion are closely connected because force is what causes changes in motion. In physics, force is the driving factor behind the movement, stopping, or change in the direction or speed of objects.

Let’s look at some important rules about motion.

topics.title: Newton’s Laws of Motion
topics.content:
Isaac Newton was a scientist who developed three laws of motion. Newton's laws of motion are three fundamental principles that describe how objects move and interact with forces. Here’s an explanation of each law with simple examples to make them easy to understand:

Newton's First Law of Motion

This is also known as the Law of Inertia.

Statement: An object at rest will stay at rest, and an object in motion will stay in motion at a constant velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

Example:

• At Rest: Imagine a book lying on a table. The book will stay there unless someone pushes it (an unbalanced force).

• In Motion: If you roll a ball on a smooth surface, it will keep rolling in a straight line at a constant speed until something stops it (like friction from the surface or hitting a wall).

topics.title: Newton’s Second Law of Motion
topics.content:
This law is also known as the Law of Acceleration.

Statement: The acceleration of an object depends on the mass of the object and the amount of force applied. This is often written as (F = ma), where (F) is force, (m) is mass, and (a) is acceleration.

Example:

• Pushing a Cart: If you push an empty shopping cart, it accelerates quickly because it has little mass. If you push a cart full of groceries with the same force, it accelerates more slowly because it has more mass. The harder you push (more force), the faster the cart will accelerate.

topics.title: Newton’s Third Law of Motion
topics.content:
This is also known as the law of reaction.

Statement: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Example:

• Walking: When you walk, your foot pushes backward against the ground. In reaction, the ground pushes your foot forward with an equal and opposite force, propelling you forward.

• Jumping off a Boat: If you jump off a small boat, you push the boat in the opposite direction. As you move forward, the boat moves backward.

topics.title: What is gravity?
topics.content:
Isaac Newton made another important discovery. A famous story tells how Newton watched an apple fall from a tree. He set out to discover why things always fall toward the ground, instead of sideways, or up! In doing so, Newton developed the law of gravity .

A ball thrown in the air comes back to the surface due to Earth's gravity. Courtesy: geeksforgeeks.org

Gravity is a force. It is what keeps us on Earth’s surface. Newton said that all matter is attracted to other matter and that larger (more massive) objects create stronger forces. Our mass is attracted to Earth’s mass, and that force (gravity) pulls us to the ground. Earth is so large compared to humans that its gravitational force keeps us on the surface. Gravity also keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and Earth orbiting the Sun!

topics.title: Mass and Weight
topics.content:
Understanding the difference between mass and weight is essential for grasping basic physical science concepts.

Here’s a simple explanation along with examples:

Mass

• Definition : Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It doesn’t change regardless of the object’s location.

• Units : Mass is measured in kilograms (kg), grams (g), etc. Example :

• Imagine a bowling ball. Whether you are holding it on Earth, taking it to the Moon, or floating with it in space, the amount of matter inside the bowling ball remains the same. Therefore, its mass is constant.

Weight

• Definition : Weight is the force exerted by gravity on an object. It can change depending on the object's location (because gravity can be stronger or weaker).

• Units : Weight is measured in newtons (N) because it’s a force. It can also be expressed in pounds (lbs) in some contexts. Example :

• The same bowling ball mentioned above will have different weights on Earth and the Moon. On Earth, it might weigh about 10 newtons (roughly 2.2 pounds). However, on the Moon, where gravity is weaker, it might weigh only about 1.6 newtons (roughly 0.35 pounds).

Courtesy: craiyon.com

This distinction helps in understanding why astronauts on the Moon can jump higher and carry heavy equipment more easily compared to on Earth. Their mass remains the same, but their weight is significantly less due to the Moon's weaker gravity.

topics.title: What is Friction?
topics.content:
Friction is a force that resists the motion of two surfaces sliding against each other. When you try to move a heavy box, friction arises between the box and the floor, opposing the movement.

Friction depends on the roughness of the surfaces and the force pressing them together. In this case, gravity pulls the box down, increasing the force between the box and the floor, which results in more friction. The heavier the box, the harder it is to move because of this increased friction.

To overcome friction, you must apply enough force to counteract its resistance.

topics.title: What is Energy?
topics.content:
We know it takes a lot of energy to go running. People pay their energy bills.

But what does energy mean in science?

Energy is the ability to do work , produce heat, or cause a change. It is what makes things move, heat up, light up, or change in some way. Using energy is an essential part of everything we do.

Even opening your eyes in the morning uses energy.

Energy is measured in a unit called a joule .

topics.title: Types of Energy
topics.content:
Energy comes in several forms.

Kinetic energy is the energy in moving things. Objects have kinetic energy when they are moving. As long as an object is moving at the same velocity, it will keep the same kinetic energy. The larger the mass or the faster it is moving, the more energy an object will have.

Electrical energy is a kind of kinetic energy. It comes from the movement of electrons we learned about in chemistry lessons. Electrical energy is in the electricity we use to give us light and power. Potential energy is the stored energy in an object.

Objects on top of slopes have potential energy.

Potential energy describes how much an object could move. A ball on top of a hill, a bucket held in the air, and a stretched spring: all of those examples have stored energy waiting to be released. The farther they have to drop, recoil, or roll, the more potential energy they have.

Chemical energy is involved in combustion

Chemical energy is a kind of potential energy. It is stored in compounds and released during chemical reactions when chemical bonds break or form. As your body digests food, the chemical reactions taking place produce chemical energy for you to use. When a fire burns, the chemical reaction produces heat energy.

topics.title: Transferring Energy
topics.content:
Energy has a very important rule. It cannot be created or destroyed, just transferred (moved from one thing to another). This rule is called the Law of Conservation of Energy. Like matter, energy is always conserved, or saved, in one form or another. It is never gone. It just changes into something else.

Energy can be transferred as work or as heat:

Work is a force applied to an object that causes the object to move. When you spend energy to kick a soccer ball, energy transfers from your body to the ball. The transfer of energy causes the ball to fly through the air (and hopefully into the goal!). The rate of doing work or consuming energy is called power, and it is measured in horsepower or watts (joules per second).

Heat is energy that transfers from an object with a higher temperature to an object with a lower temperature.

When you use energy to heat your oven, energy transfers from the heating coils to the air in your oven, making the air in the oven hotter.

topics.title: Converting Energy
topics.content:
As energy is transferred, it can be converted, or changed, into other forms of energy. Your body is able to change the chemical energy in food into movement, which is kinetic energy. Potential energy can be converted into kinetic energy: when you drop a book, it falls. Its potential energy becomes kinetic energy. Once the book hits the ground, all of its potential energy has been converted to kinetic energy. The kinetic energy is absorbed by the ground that the book hits.

It works in the other direction, too. Kinetic energy can be converted into potential energy. Suppose that a ball is rolled to the top of a ramp. While it was rolling, it had kinetic energy, but once it has stopped at the top of the ramp, all of its energy is now potential energy.

Converting energy into electricity

Every day, huge amounts of energy are converted into electrical energy for us to use. Then we convert that electricity into other forms of energy, such as heat and light.

The image above explains the conversion of Kinetic Energy into Electrical Energy. As the turbine moves due to the force of water, it creates energy that lights the bulb. Courtesy: Animated Science

topics.title: Using Machines
topics.content:
In your test, you may get questions about simple machines. Machines are things that help people to do work. People have been using simple machines for thousands of years to help them move things.

W=Fs

Work, W , is the amount of energy needed to move something. It is measured in Newtons –  the amount of force, F , applied over a distance, s .

An advantage is something that gives you extra help.

Mechanical advantage, IMA, is a measure of how much help a machine gives: in other words, how much it multiplies the effort (force) put into it. Mechanical advantage is the slope divided by the height.

Examples of simple machines that give us mechanical advantages are:

• Ramps: Ramps, or slopes, make it easier to raise heavy loads. It’s easier to push loads up a slope than to lift them. But it takes longer. A ramp reduces the amount of work by increasing the distance that needs to be covered. The longer the slope, the easier the work.

• Levers: A lever is a bar resting on a fulcrum. A fulcrum (green triangle in the image) is the point at which the lever tips one way or the other. A lever can move a heavy load with one end when pressure is applied to the other. The amount of force that is needed depends on the weight of the load and where the fulcrum is positioned.

• Pulley s are another kind of simple machine. Pulleys use wheels and ropes to reduce the force needed to lift an object.

Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

GED EXAM TIP: Making the right calculation to answer Physics questions You know by now that the information you need to answer questions is almost always in front of you. Much of the work in your test is making sure you understand what information to use. It’s the same with the questions that require math. Physics questions often use math, so we are going to practice with another math question in this test tip. The math is usually easy, but you need to know which numbers to use and what to do with them. ■ Check for understanding Let’s use some math to calculate force and mechanical advantage. It takes 100 newtons (N) of force to lift a small box straight up to 2 meters (m) (the height of the big blue box in the picture). But you have a ramp. The ramp is 10 m long. The mechanical advantage is the length of the slope divided by the height of the box, or 10 m divided by 2 m. 10/2 = 5, so the mechanical advantage is 5. This advantage of 5 means it takes you 5 times less effort to push the box up the ramp than it would to lift it. The force you need is the original force divided by the mechanical advantage. Instead of 100 N, it takes only 20 N (100/5 = 20) to move the little box to the top of the big blue box. Now suppose the height of the big blue box is still 2 m, but this time the length of your ramp is only 4 m. What is the mechanical advantage of the 4–meter ramp? And how many newtons would it take to move the small box to the top of the big blue box using the 4–meter ramp? To answer, let’s do the calculation again, but using 4 instead of 10. The length of the slope divided by the height of the slope is 4 m divided by 2 m. 4/2 = 2. So the mechanical advantage is 2. The original force is still 100 newtons because the height of the big box is still 2 m. To find out how many newtons it will take to get the little box up to the top, divide the force (100) by the advantage (2). 100/2 is 50. It would take 50 N to get the box up. So although the question involved the difficult topics of force and work, the answer took just a simple calculation. But you needed your reasoning skills to know which calculation to make. Your reasoning skills told you to apply the rules given in the background text.

topics.title: Words to know
topics.content:
**Calculate** — figure out by doing a sum

**Convert** — change into something else; when you change a measurement from one unit to another, the quantity is the same, but the unit you measure it with changes

**Formula** — mathematical rule or recipe you can apply in science; formulas use symbols, such as “s” for speed, that can be replaced with units of measurement in equations

**Metric** — something measured or counted in parts or multiples of ten

**Standard** — some agreed and used as the accepted measurement or level

**Unit** — fixed quantity used for measuring other quantities of the same thing

topics.title: Units of measurement
topics.content:
Units are standardized amounts used to measure various aspects of the world around us.

Here are some important units we learned during the last few lessons:

• Time : Hours (h) : Measures longer durations, with 24 hours in a day. Minutes (min) : Smaller unit, with 60 minutes in an hour.

• Distance : Miles (mi) : Common in the U.S. for long distances, like driving. Kilometers (km) : Used in many countries; 1 mile is about 1.609 km.

• Mass : Kilograms (kg) : Standard unit for mass in the metric system, used for measuring weight. Grams (g) : Smaller unit; 1 kg equals 1,000 g, often used in cooking.

• Weight : Newtons (N) : Measures weight as the force of gravity on an object. Pounds (lb) : Commonly used in the U.S., where 1 lb is about 0.45 kg.

• Energy : Joules (J) : Standard unit of energy, measuring work done. Calories (cal) : Measures the energy content of food; 1 cal is about 4.184 J.

Some units, like hours and miles, we use all the time in our daily lives. Others, like newtons and joules, you will see in your science test.

There are different size units to measure the same things, depending on how big they are. In daily life, we don’t want to measure a whole lifetime in hours, so we use years. You don’t want to measure the length of your finger in miles, so you use inches.

topics.title: Converting Units
topics.content:
You can convert units from one size to another. Scientists convert units because they DO want to measure everything in fixed units. This avoids confusion. Scientists have chosen certain units to be standard .

Here are some standard units you may see in your test, together with their letter symbols.

In your test, you can multiply or divide units to convert them into the standard units shown above. For example, it says in the table above that time is measured in seconds. You know there are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour. So you can convert hours and minutes to seconds by multiplying.

topics.title: Metric Units
topics.content:
Scientists generally use metric units. These are meters instead of miles and kilograms instead of pounds. Most countries in the world use the metric system, so you may have used metric measurements in your country of origin. Metric units are easier to convert because they are in units of 10. Here is a table that shows the beginning of the words in metric units.

This table shows the meaning of word beginnings used in metric measurements. Kilo– tells you it is 1,000 of something (for example, a kilogram is 1,000 grams). Centi– tells you it is one hundredth (1/100) of something (for example, a centimeter is 1/100 of a meter).

topics.title: Formulas
topics.content:
Formulas are rules or recipes used in science. You can apply formulas to find measurements of time, distance, force, and many other things. Scientists use symbols for those things, just like they do for elements in chemistry.

For example, the symbol for time is t, and the symbol for force is F . If you have already taken the math course, you have probably solved formulas or equations, however, let’s review again.

Let’s look at a simple formula.

The formula for speed is:

{$s=\frac{d}{t}$}

where speed (symbol: s) equals distance (symbol: d) divided by time (symbol: t).

How can we use it?

If you walk a distance of 6 kilometers (km) in a time of 3 hours, you might want to know how fast you walked. You can use the formula s=d/t. Plug in the numbers you already know in place of the symbols. That would be s = 6/3.

Now we have an equation we can solve. Our equation says speed equals 6 km divided by 3 hours which is 2 kilometers per hour.

topics.title: Symbols in Physics
topics.content:
Symbols and formulas are fundamental components of physics that provide a concise way to represent physical concepts and relationships.

• Symbols : In physics, symbols are used to denote various physical quantities, such as mass (m), velocity (v), force (F), energy (E), and time (t). These symbols create a universal language that allows scientists and engineers to communicate complex ideas succinctly.

• Formulas : Formulas are mathematical equations that express relationships between different physical quantities. For example, Newton’s second law of motion is represented by the formula F=m

⋅a, where F is

force, m is mass, and a is acceleration. Formulas allow for the calculation and prediction of physical behavior in various scenarios.

Together, symbols and formulas enable students and professionals to analyze, interpret, and solve problems in the physical world, forming the foundation of scientific inquiry and technological development. Understanding these elements is crucial for anyone studying or working in the field of physics.

A note about multiply and divide signs:

The multiply sign (x) is often replaced with a dot • in physics. So you may, sometimes, see m • a, instead of m x a.

But other times, there is nothing between the two multipliers. PW = T means P x W = T.

The divide sign you see in mathematics (÷) is often replaced by /.

So P/W = T means P ÷ W = T.

topics.title: Changing Formulas
topics.content:
You can change formulas around to solve equations in your test. In fact, the formula is an equation itself: like chemistry equations or math equations, both sides of the equation must be equal. If you take something away or divide it on one side, you need to take it away or divide it on the other side as well. This means:

• If F = m ( a ), then a = F/m and m = F/a

• If P = W / t, then W = P ( t )

• If p = m (v ), then v = p/m

• If d = s ( t ), then s = d/t – the formula we used above!

topics.title: Applying Formulas in Physics
topics.content:
If you follow the formula’s recipe, you can find the answer you need. In your science test, this may mean calculating speed, distance, or acceleration. Or you may be asked to figure out how much work was done in joules.

You do not need to remember the formulas because your test will always give you the formula you need. It doesn’t matter if you don’t understand the science behind the formulas. You don’t even have to remember all the units of measurement. But you do need to know how to use the formula.

So how? If you are given a formula, use it to create an equation with the pieces you already know, you already know that equations are mathematical sums that you have to balance. You may need to change formulas around to fit the question. Then solve the equation to find the missing piece, or answer.

topics.title: Video: Using Formulas to Answer Physics Questions
topics.content:
Watch the video, then take the optional quiz.

Using Formulas to Answer Questions on the GED Exam We’ve looked at a couple of simple examples in the lesson. For your test tip, we’re going to practice a more difficult question, but it’s okay! We are going to use the same steps. You will need a calculator unless you are very good at dividing.

(You will use a calculator in your test for questions like this.) An object has a weight of 5.10 Newtons (N) at sea level, where the acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s2. What is the acceleration due to gravity on the object in a spaceship 1,000 km above sea level, where gravity exerts a force of 3.81 N on the object? Formula: F (Newtons) = m (kg) x a (m/ s2) 1.33 m/s2 2.57 m/s2 7.33 m/s2 12.6 m/s2 Let’s take a deep breath and figure out what we know and what we need to do. First, what did the question tell us? It told us the force (weight in Newtons) at sea level, and it told us the acceleration there in m/s2. It also gave us the formula we need to answer the question! And not just the formula, but the units of measurement too. We know that the Newtons in the question are measuring weight/force (F) and that (a) must be acceleration because it’s measured in m/s2. Finally, it gave us a measurement we don’t need: 1,000 km above sea level. Although the height changes the force of gravity, we don’t actually use it in answering the question. What did the question not tell us? It did not tell us that in physics, weight is different from mass. In physics, weight is a force. You will need to remember that for your test. Also, it did not tell us the mass (m) of the object. You will need to figure out the mass before you can answer the question about acceleration. What is the question asking us to do? It’s asking us to find a quantity of something. That something is the acceleration of the object at a different gravity. So we’re going to use the information we have (some numbers and a formula) to make an equation that will give us the answer. What shall we do first? We’ll use the formula to work out the mass of the object. When you do this at home, it will help to have a piece of paper and a pencil or pen. Then you can write down your formula in different ways as you switch the parts around. And you can line up numbers under your formula when you put in the numbers you have. The formula says F (Newtons) equals mass (kg) x acceleration, or F = m • a. But we already know F. Let’s turn the formula around to get the right formula for m: Mass equals force divided by acceleration, or m = f/a. Does it still balance? Yes. So for our equation, that means m = 5.10 /9.81. Use your calculator to divide 5.10 by 9.81. 5.10 /9.81 = 0.52 So we know m = 0.52 kg. Mass will be the same for the next part of the problem because mass does not change with gravity. Now let’s answer the question: What is the acceleration due to gravity on the object … where gravity exerts a force of 3.81 N on the object? We’ve got mass (0.52 kg) and force (3.81 N) but we need to find acceleration. How do we calculate the acceleration with a different force? Let’s go back to our formula and switch it around again, so it can give us the formula for acceleration (a). Our formula is F = m • a, but we already know F. We need to know what an equals, so let’s change it to read a = F/m. Now we can plug in the numbers we already have for F and m. Using our numbers to make an equation, we get: a = F/m or 3.81/0.52. Use your calculator to divide 3.81 by 0.52. 3.81/0.52 = 7.33. Now we can look back at the answers, and confirm our calculations are right. Answer (C) says 7.33 m/s2. So, (C) is the right answer. We did some careful reading, quite a bit of thinking, and then two division sums to get this answer. The division was easy with a calculator. In fact, figuring out what we needed to do was a lot harder than doing the math. We had to use reasoning skills to know which numbers to use. Your science test wants you to demonstrate your reasoning skills, and that’s why we chose this question for your exam tip. This question is from the GED official practice test.

topics.title: About This Lesson
topics.content: Preparing for your Science Test and Final Practice Quiz You have learned many science skills in this class! This last lesson will prepare you to take your test. We’ll review what you need to know and give you some last tips. In this lesson, we’ll review helpful exam tips, like back-solving, elimination, and estimation. We will also review science knowledge that you should know and remember for your GED exam. For example, you will need to know how to read graphs and charts that show scientific data. We will also review the main parts of the scientific method and science topics that will be covered in the Science portion of the GED Exam. At the end of this review lesson, you will test your science knowledge by taking a short quiz.

topics.title: Science to Learn and Remember
topics.content:
Throughout your study, we've emphasized that the information needed to answer questions will be provided to you. However, it's also important to grasp some basic science concepts that can help you succeed.

You should focus on understanding key science concepts, reading graphs and charts that display scientific data, and using reasoning to interpret scientific information effectively.

Remember: The science test is not just about memorization! For example, you won’t need to memorize the entire periodic table of elements, but you will need to recognize the names and symbols of key elements to answer some questions correctly.

In the following pages, we will provide you with a checklist of important things to remember for your test. Some items will include essential facts and processes, while many will consist of terms you should be able to recognize.

topics.title: Basic Terms to Remember
topics.content:
• Variables are things that are different or can change. There are two kinds of variables : Independent variables are the ones you start with in an experiment. Scientists may apply or change variables to see what effect they have. Dependent variables are the results of performing your experiment. They are changes that depend on the independent variables.

• Averages: There are three types of average s: The mean is the sum of all the numbers in a set divided by the number of numbers that were added together. The median is the number in the middle of a set of numbers when they are in order from the smallest to largest. The mode is the number that appears most often in a set of numbers.

topics.title: Living Things
topics.content:
Biology is the study of living things (life).

• Living things ( organisms ) are made up of tiny parts called cells . All cells have a nucleus containing DNA. Cells perform many different jobs.

• Two ways that cells reproduce are mitosis (splitting in two to make new cells) and meiosis (combining cells with the cells of another living thing to create a new organism).

• Heredity is the process by which living things pass their traits to their descendants. Children get one set of genes (sequences of DNA) from each parent. If one of the pair of genes for a trait is dominant, that will be the one that shows in the child.

• Evolution happens when DNA and traits change as they are passed down through generations. In evolution, the term fitness means the ability to survive and reproduce. Natural selection means that more fit members of a species survive and pass on their traits. Over many thousands of years, evolution can produce new species.

• Resources are the things all organisms need to survive.

• The environment is everything around us. Humans affect Earth’s environment and resources through development, farming, pollution, and climate change.

• Ecosystems are sets of living and nonliving things that function together. All organisms interact with others to survive.

• The different ways that energy moves through an ecosystem from one organism to another is called a food web .

• Producers are organisms, such as plants, that make their own energy (food). Consumers are organisms that receive energy from other organisms.

topics.title: The Planet Earth
topics.content:
• Earth’s crust is broken up into slow–moving tectonic plates . These plates float on the mantle and fit together to form Earth’s rocky surface.

• Minerals are non–living substances found on Earth.

• The atmosphere is a layer of gasses around Earth that keeps the planet warm. The gases include nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide. When fossil fuels burn, they send carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

• Climate means weather patterns over a long period of time. Scientists believe that increasing amounts of carbon dioxide and other gasses in the atmosphere are making Earth warmer and changing Earth’s climate.

• Earth is part of a system of planets called the solar system . The other planets are Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Neptune, Saturn, Uranus, and Venus.

• The planets orbit the Sun, which is the center of our solar system and the source of Earth’s light and heat. Our solar system is in a galaxy called the Milky Way. There are billions of galaxies in the universe.

• The early astronomers developed theories about space by using observation and mathematics. The invention of the telescope helped prove their theories right or wrong.

topics.title: Chemistry
topics.content:
Chemistry is the study of what things are made of, how they behave, and how they change.

• Matter is every living and non–living thing. Matter is composed of atoms . Atoms contain protons , neutrons , and electrons .

• Elements are matter made of one kind of atom. The atomic number of an element is the number of protons in its atoms.

• The atomic mass of an atom is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

• Electrons have a negative charge. Protons have a positive charge. Neutrons have no charge. The opposite charges attract each other. A charged atom (one with an electric charge) is called an ion .

• A molecule is a clump of atoms. Chemical bonds hold molecules together.

• Solids, liquids, and gases are three phases of matter . Changes from one state to another are physical changes .

• A chemical change happens when the substance changes into a different substance. The process that causes this is called a chemical reaction. Combustion (burning) is a chemical reaction.

• Nothing goes away in a chemical reaction. Everything at the beginning of a chemical change is still there after the chemical reaction takes place but in a different form.

• Reactants are substances that start a chemical reaction. Products are substances that come out after a chemical reaction. Catalysts are things that make chemical reactions happen or speed them up.

• In a chemical formula, the subscript (little number) tells you how many atoms that molecule has. The coefficient (big number) tells you how many of a particular molecule are combined to make a particular substance.

• Chemical equations must always be balanced by showing the same number of atoms before and after the reaction.

• Oxygen’s symbol is O, carbon is C, and hydrogen is H. The formula for oxygen gas is O 2 , water is H 2 O, and carbon dioxide is CO 2 . You don’t have to memorize them, but those would be the most useful symbols and formulas to recognize for your test.

topics.title: Physics
topics.content:
Physics is the study of matter, including how they move.

• Newton’s laws of motion are rules that explain how things move.

• Velocity is speed in a certain direction.

• Acceleration is a change in speed or velocity over time.

• Momentum is the amount of motion in a moving object.

• Force is the push or pull on an object that happens because of another object.

• Gravity is a force that keeps us on Earth’s surface.

• Mass is the amount of matter in something.

• Weight is gravity and mass combined.

• Friction is a force that results when two objects move alongside one another.

• Energy is the ability to do work or produce heat. Energy can not be created or destroyed. It can be stored, transferred, or converted into other forms of energy.

• Formulas are recipes used to find measurements of time, distance, force, and many other things. You can change the parts around to solve equations, but the equation must stay balanced.

topics.title: Test Questions
topics.content:
All along, you have been practicing for your test. You have answered questions at the end of each lesson. There will be questions like these on your test.

The GED ® science is 90 minutes long, with questions across three main topics: Earth and space science, life science, and physical science .

As with the other GED exams, the science exam is scored from 100-200, with a passing score set at 145 or higher.

topics.title: GED Exam Tip
topics.content:
Exam tip In this course, you have read many new words. But can you remember what they all mean? If possible, memorize them just like you have memorized your multiplication tables. Re–read the “words to know” section at the beginning of every lesson. Form a mental picture of what each term means; you will know what it means without having to think about it. Remember that the GED exam may ask you to make

calculations based on scientific data. You should know some common formulas that will help you with the calculations. Some common formulas to review are: Distance equals space times time: d = s (t) Force equals mass times acceleration: F = m (a) Power equals work divided by time: P = W / t Work equals force times displacement: W = F(s) Einstein's formula, energy equals mass times the speed of light squared: E = mc² Also, you should know Newton's three laws of motion: Newton’s First Law of Motion (Also known as the Law of Inertia) : An object at rest will remain at rest unless acted on by an external force. An object in motion will continue in the same motion unless acted on by an external force. Newton’s Second Law of Motion : Force equals mass times acceleration, written as the formula F = m(a) Newton’s Third Law of Motion: For every action (or force), there is an equal and opposite reaction (or force). But you have learned all the skills you need to answer the questions! After the quiz, we’ll show you how to get ready for the test.
